course.title: Physics: Motion and Forces
course.description: Move a cart, balance a force and follow the energy. Predict what happens next.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with signed numbers, ratios, basic algebra and square roots. No previous physics course is assumed.

paragraphs: Mechanics is the part of physics that explains how things move and what makes them move. It starts from things you can watch, such as a ball in flight or a cyclist braking. People study it because the same few ideas apply to cars, bridges, sports and spacecraft, and because most other branches of physics are built on it.

The course has 18 lessons in six parts. The first two describe motion with positions, velocities and accelerations, and teach you to predict where a moving cart will be. The next two bring in forces, from balanced forces and Newton's second law to weight, friction and the way objects push back on each other. The last two follow energy, power and momentum, which let you answer questions about collisions and about how much work a machine really does.
Each lesson explains an idea first and asks about it afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs. Numbers are part of the work, and a calculator is welcome.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a change in position from the distance travelled, and find an average velocity from a trip or a graph.
You'll be able to predict the velocity and position of an object that speeds up or slows down at a steady rate.
You'll be able to use Newton's laws to find the acceleration that a set of forces produces.
You'll be able to find the work a force does and follow energy between motion, height and heat.
You'll be able to use momentum and impulse to predict the speeds after a collision.

lessons.title: Where did it go?

steps.headline: Saying where something is

lead.text: Back in the corridor, we need a way to say where you are with a single number. The trick is to measure from a mark. Choose the door and call it zero, then measure in metres from there, as if a tape measure lay along the floor with its zero end at the door. That starting mark is called the origin, and you can put it wherever suits the job.

A number alone does not say which side of the origin you are on, so we also choose a positive direction. Say it points towards the far end of the corridor. A spot 5 metres along it has the position +5 m. A spot 4 metres behind the door, out in the street, has the position −4 m. The sign gives the side and the number gives how far from the origin.

afterFigure.text: Both choices are ours to make. Two people watching the same walk can pick different origins, or opposite positive directions, and both be right as long as each keeps to their own choice. Once the choices are made, a position is a single signed number. The same idea works up and down: with the ground floor as the origin and up as positive, the basement of a building is a negative position. With that in place we can describe a move from one place to another.

steps.headline: The change in position

lead.text: Now let the walk begin. You start at the door, which is position 0. You finish at the 5 m mark. That is a change in position. Subtract the starting position from the finishing one and you have its size and its direction, which physics calls the displacement.

Try it on a walker who goes from 1 m to 4 m. Finishing minus starting is 4 − 1 = +3 m. The plus sign says the walker moved towards larger positions, which is our positive direction. The 3 says by how much. If the same walker goes back from 4 m to 1 m, the sum is 1 − 4 = −3 m. The size is unchanged and the sign flips, because the move now goes the other way.

afterFigure.text: Look at what the sum uses. It takes the place where the walker began and the place where it finished, and nothing in between. A walker who took a long route and came back gets the same displacement as one who walked straight there. That makes displacement a tidy answer to where something ended up compared with where it began. How much ground a trip covers needs more than its two ends, and we come to that after some practice.

lead.text: A dot slides along a track from the 2 m mark to the 9 m mark. Right is the positive direction.

reveal.text: You subtracted the start from the finish: 9 − 2. The plus sign says the dot moved in the positive direction.

lead.text: Now run the same sum when the move goes the other way, and keep the sign.

steps.headline: The ground a trip covers

lead.text: Go back to the walk that opened the lesson: 5 metres along the corridor, then 2 metres back. Its displacement is 3 − 0 = +3 m, since you finished at the 3 m mark and began at 0. A pedometer in your pocket would give a different total, because it counts every step in either direction. It would show 7 metres.

That second number is the distance: the total length of the path you followed. To find it, cut the path wherever you turn round, take each stretch as a plain length and add them up. The 5 m out and the 2 m back both count, and turning round gives no refund for the way back. Distance has no direction, so it is never negative.

afterFigure.text: So one trip has two honest descriptions. Displacement compares where you finished with where you began, and it can be positive, negative or zero. Distance adds up the ground covered, and it can only grow as the trip goes on. The two have the same size only when the trip never turns round. The picture sets a trip that doubles back beside one that goes straight, so you can compare them.

cases.label: Out and back: 0 m, 5 m, then 3 m

steps.headline: A trolley goes from 1 m to 5 m, then back to 2 m. Find its displacement and its distance.

workedSteps.text: Displacement uses only the ends: finish minus start.
Distance adds the stretches. The way out runs from 1 m to 5 m.
The way back runs from 5 m to 2 m, which is 3 m. Add the two stretches.

steps.headline: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What distance does it cover?

workedSteps.text: The way out runs from 1 m to 7 m.
The way back is the same length.
Add the two stretches.

steps.headline: Moving the origin

lead.text: One more check on our measuring set-up: does the choice of origin change the answers? Two friends watch the same walker. One lays a tape with its zero at the door. The other lays a second tape with its zero 10 metres behind the door, so every position she reads is 10 m larger than the first friend's.

Suppose the walker goes from the 3 m mark to the 8 m mark on the first tape. The second tape reads 13 m and 18 m for the same two places. Every reading has shifted by 10, yet the displacement is 8 − 3 = 5 m on one tape and 18 − 13 = 5 m on the other. The shift appears in both terms of the subtraction, so it cancels.

afterFigure.text: This is why we can put the origin wherever it makes the sums easiest. A single position only means something once you know where the origin was, whereas a displacement is the same for everyone who watches the trip. Distance agrees for everyone too, because it is a length along the path and the path does not care where the tape starts.

lead.text: Two students record one trip. The first reads it as 2 m to 9 m. The second has her zero 10 m behind the first student's zero, so each of her readings is 10 m larger.
A robot drives along a straight track and turns round partway.

reveal.text: The robot's displacement is only +3 m, yet it covered 13 m. The turn makes the two numbers differ.

blocks.text: Picture a long straight corridor with a door at one end. You step out through that door and walk 5 metres along the corridor. Then you remember something you left behind, turn round and walk 2 metres back. A friend waiting at the door has watched the whole thing.

Ask the friend two questions and you get two different answers. Ask how much ground your feet covered and they will say 7 metres, the sum of the two walks. Ask where you are now and they will point at a spot 3 metres from the door, without counting the steps that got you there.
Physics gives these two answers separate names so they never get mixed up. We'll follow this walk to see what each one measures and why you need both.

intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea about motion starts from where things are and how that changes.

recap.keyIdea: Displacement is final position minus initial position, with a sign. Distance adds every stretch of the path.

blocks.text: You found that 5 m out and 2 m back leaves you 3 m from the door after 7 m of walking. You also saw that moving the origin changes every position but leaves the displacement alone.

recap.nextHook: Nothing in the corridor has a clock yet. Next we time the walk and ask how quickly the position changes.

lessons.title: Speed and direction

steps.headline: Ground covered each second

lead.text: Take the dash from the opener: 20 metres in 4 seconds. Share the ground out over the time and you get 5 metres for every second. A number like that is the average speed of the trip, found by dividing the distance travelled by the time it took.

The unit follows from the sum. Metres divided by seconds gives metres per second, written m/s, so 5 m/s means 5 metres of ground for each second that passes. The word average matters. A cyclist who dawdled at the start and sprinted at the end could cover the same 20 metres in the same 4 seconds, and the sum would still give 5 m/s. It describes the trip as a whole and says nothing about any single moment.

afterFigure.text: Here is a second example, a runner who covers 12 metres in 3 seconds. Dividing gives 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m/s. Stretch the same 12 metres over 6 seconds and the answer halves to 2 m/s, which matches what you would see, because the runner is moving more slowly. The distance in this sum is the total path length from the last lesson, so it never carries a sign. That leaves open what to do when the direction matters.

lead.text: A rover drives straight for 6 seconds and covers 18 metres. It need not keep one pace the whole way.

reveal.text: You divided the distance by the time. That is an average: the rover may have been faster and slower along the way.

steps.headline: Adding a direction

lead.text: Average speed forgets which way you went. That suits a pedometer, but the last lesson showed that direction matters, because displacement keeps it as a sign. Divide the displacement by the time instead of the distance and you get the average velocity.

A cyclist whose displacement is +8 m in 2 s has an average velocity of +4 m/s. A cyclist who ends up 9 metres behind the start after 3 seconds has an average velocity of −9 ÷ 3 = −3 m/s. The sign says which way along the line the trip went, and the number says how fast.

afterFigure.text: On a straight trip that never turns round, the displacement and the distance have the same size. The average speed is then the size of the average velocity, and the only difference is the sign. That is why speed is never negative while velocity can be. The two come apart once a trip doubles back, and a later screen looks at that.

lead.text: A cart rolls to the left. Left is the negative direction, so the displacement has a minus sign.

steps.headline: When the two averages differ

lead.text: Now let the trip turn round. Suppose you walk 30 m to a shop and straight back, and the whole round trip takes 20 s. The distance is 30 + 30 = 60 m, so the average speed is 60 ÷ 20 = 3 m/s. That matches how brisk the walk felt.

The displacement tells a different story. You finished where you started, so finishing minus starting is 0 m. The average velocity is 0 ÷ 20 = 0 m/s. The way out counts as positive and the way back as negative, so in displacement they cancel. In distance they cannot cancel, because every stretch adds.

afterFigure.text: This is the sense in which velocity and speed differ. Speed asks how much ground is covered each second. Velocity asks how fast the position is changing in a particular direction, so a trip that ends at its start has an average velocity of zero no matter how fast it went. From here on we keep both, and use whichever the question needs.

cases.label: Shop and back: 60 m in 20 s

steps.headline: A trolley goes 15 m right in 3 s, then 5 m left in 2 s. Find both averages.

workedSteps.text: Add the lengths of the stretches and add the times. Average speed divides the total distance by the total time.
Displacement is the net move, with right positive.
Average velocity divides the displacement by the same total time.

lead.text: A runner heads out along a straight road and then comes straight back to the marker where the run began.

reveal.text: The finish equals the start, so the displacement is zero. Distance and displacement part company on a return trip.

steps.headline: A trip made of stretches

lead.text: Many trips come in stretches at different paces, and the average for the whole trip needs care. Suppose a jogger covers 10 m in 2 s, then slows and covers the next 10 m in 8 s. The first stretch is 5 m/s and the second is 1.25 m/s. It is tempting to average those two numbers and get about 3.1 m/s.

That answer is too high. The jogger spent four times as long on the slow stretch as on the fast one, so the slow stretch should count for more. Go back to the definition and use the totals: 20 m of ground in 2 + 8 = 10 s gives 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s. The rule is the same every time, the total distance over the total time, whatever the stretches looked like.

afterFigure.text: The same rule works for average velocity: the total displacement over the total time. When a trip is made of stretches, add up the stretches first and divide once at the end.

lead.text: A cyclist rides two equal stretches, but the second takes longer than the first.

reveal.text: The whole trip is 24 m in 8 s. The mean of the two stretch speeds is 4 m/s, which gives too much weight to the faster stretch.

blocks.text: Last lesson's corridor had no clock in it. Put one there. A friend stands at a mark 20 metres from the door with a stopwatch, and you set off from the door on a bicycle at a steady pace. They start the watch as you go and stop it as you pass them. It reads 4 seconds.

That reading adds something new. The corridor tells us how much ground the trip covered. The stopwatch tells us how long it took. Put together, they say how fast you went. They also let us compare trips: a friend who covered the 20 metres in 5 seconds was slower.

Things get more interesting once the trip turns round. Cycle to the far mark and come straight back to the door, and your friend can say you were moving quickly and also that you ended up where you began. Both remarks are true, and they come from two different calculations. Sorting them out starts with the straight dash.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find average speed and average velocity from a trip, and say when they differ.

recap.keyIdea: Average speed is total distance over total time. Average velocity is total displacement over total time, so it carries a sign and is zero on a trip that ends where it began.

blocks.text: You turned 20 m in 4 s into 5 m for each second. You then saw that a return trip has an average velocity of 0 even though ground was covered, and that the average for a trip made of stretches comes from the totals.

recap.nextHook: A table of positions and times is slow to read. Next we draw position against time and see what the shape of the line says about speed and direction.

lessons.title: Read a motion graph

steps.headline: Time along, position up

lead.text: Here is how the sketch is drawn. Time runs along the horizontal axis, starting at 0 on the left. Position goes up the vertical axis, measured from the origin as in the first lesson. Each pair of readings from the table becomes one dot, placed above its time at the height of its position. A sketch made this way is called a position–time graph.

Take a walker who covers 2 metres every second. At 1 s the dot sits at 2 m. At 2 s it sits at 4 m, and at 3 s it sits at 6 m. The dots lie on a straight line, and that is no accident. When the position changes by the same amount each second, the dots line up. Joining them gives a straight line.

afterFigure.text: The second case in the picture is a faster walker, who covers 4 metres every second. The line is still straight, but it climbs more quickly. Keep an eye on how the line leans, because the lean carries the information in the rest of this lesson.

lead.text: Back to the friend in the corridor, who keeps a steady pace away from the door.

steps.headline: How steep the line is

lead.text: The lean of a line is called its slope, and here it has a simple meaning. Pick two points on a straight line. The rise is how far the line goes up between them, which is the change in position. The run is how far it goes along, which is the change in time. Slope is the rise divided by the run.

Change in position divided by change in time is the quantity from the last lesson: the velocity. So the slope of a position–time graph is the velocity. A line from 1 m at 0 s up to 10 m at 3 s rises 9 m over a run of 3 s, which gives a slope of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s. A steeper line means a faster move.

afterFigure.text: The slope of a straight line is the same wherever you measure it, so you can pick whichever two points are easiest to read. That is what makes the graph a quick way to get a velocity. You read two points, subtract on each axis and divide.

lead.text: A straight line on a position–time graph runs from 2 m at 0 s up to 14 m at 3 s.

reveal.text: You divided the rise by the run. That quotient is the velocity along the segment.

steps.headline: Flat lines and falling lines

lead.text: So far every line has climbed. Two other shapes matter. If the position stays at 6 m for a few seconds, the dots sit at the same height and the line runs flat. A flat line has a rise of zero, so its slope is zero. The object has stopped at that spot.

If the position gets smaller as time passes, the line slopes downwards. Take a line from 14 m at 0 s to 2 m at 4 s. The rise is 2 − 14 = −12 m over a run of 4 s, so the slope is −12 ÷ 4 = −3 m/s. The minus sign means the object is moving in the negative direction, back towards the origin.

afterFigure.text: One graph can now tell a whole story. The shoelace walk from the start of the lesson draws a line that rises while the friend sets off. It runs flat during the stop and falls on the way back. Reading a graph like this means going through it a stretch at a time and asking what the slope of each stretch is.

lead.text: A walker heads back towards the origin, so the line on the graph slopes down.

reveal.text: Final minus initial is negative, so the velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction.

steps.headline: A trolley is out for 2 s, still for 2 s and back for 2 s. Find its velocity in each stretch.

workedSteps.text: The first stretch rises from 0 m to 8 m in 2 s. Divide the rise by the run.
The middle stretch is flat, so the position holds.
The last stretch falls from 8 m to 2 m in 2 s.

steps.headline: One number for the whole trip

lead.text: A graph with several stretches has several velocities, but sometimes you want one number for the entire trip. That is the average velocity we met earlier, and the graph makes it easy to find. Look only at the first point and the last point, and ignore everything in between.

Suppose a walker starts at 1 m at 0 s and finishes at 7 m at 10 s, after a pause and a short detour on the way. The rise from end to end is 7 − 1 = 6 m over a run of 10 s, so the average velocity is 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6 m/s. The pause and the detour still use up time, and that is why the average is slow.

afterFigure.text: You do not need the middle of the graph for this. Displacement depends only on where the trip began and where it ended, so the end points are enough. The straight line in the picture has the same slope as the whole winding trip.

lead.text: The trolley from the worked example is back on the graph: out, a pause, then a return. Only its start, its finish and the total time matter for the average.

reveal.text: The pause and the turn still use up time, so they pull the average velocity down to 1/3 m/s.

blocks.text: A friend walks away from you down the corridor while you note where they are at each second. After 2 seconds they are 3 metres from the door. After 4 seconds they are at 6 metres. You jot each pair of numbers in a table, and by the end of a minute the table is long.

Two quite different walks could produce a table that long. One friend strolled steadily the whole way. The other set off briskly, stopped to tie a shoelace and then wandered back. Reading the rows one at a time to tell which walk you have is slow work, and it is easy to lose track of what the numbers are doing.

A sketch fixes that. Plot each reading as a dot and join the dots, and the shape of the line shows how the walk went. We'll learn to draw a trip that way and then to read its story back out of the shape.

recap.keyIdea: On a position–time graph, slope is velocity: steep is fast, flat is stopped and falling is negative. The average velocity of a whole trip needs only its end points.

blocks.text: You turned 3 m after 2 s into 9 m after 6 s, and read a flat stretch as a stop and a falling one as motion in the negative direction. Over a trip with a pause and a turn you found an average velocity of just 1/3 m/s.

recap.nextHook: So far the velocity has stayed fixed along each stretch. Next it starts to change, and we need a name for how quickly it does.

lessons.title: Changing velocity

steps.headline: Velocity that keeps changing

lead.text: Return to the traffic lights. Suppose the car gains 3 metres per second of velocity during every second that passes. At the start it is at rest. After 1 s the needle reads 3 m/s, after 2 s it reads 6 m/s and after 3 s it reads 9 m/s. The reading rises by the same amount each second, and that amount is the number we are after.

How quickly the velocity changes is called acceleration. For this car it is 3 metres per second, every second, which is written 3 m/s². The unit tells the story: a velocity in m/s changes, and it does so over a stretch of seconds, so seconds appear twice. A larger acceleration means the velocity changes faster. A car with an acceleration of 1 m/s² would need 9 s to reach the 9 m/s that ours reaches in 3.

afterFigure.text: Acceleration answers the question that the speedometer leaves open. Velocity tells you how the position is changing right now. Acceleration tells you how that velocity is changing right now. The next screens turn that idea into a sum.

lead.text: A different car is already rolling when the driver presses the accelerator.

steps.headline: Working out the acceleration

lead.text: Often you are given two velocities and the time between them, and the acceleration has to be found. Take the change in velocity, which is the finishing velocity minus the starting one, and divide it by the time the change took.

Say a cyclist speeds up from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 3 s. The change in velocity is 16 − 4 = 12 m/s, spread over 3 s, so the acceleration is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m/s². This is an average, like the average velocity we found earlier. The velocity might not have changed at an even rate, and the sum gives only the overall rate for the stretch.

afterFigure.text: The sum works for any pair of velocities, so it also works when they are negative. That matters in a moment, because a negative velocity is just motion in the negative direction. First, try the sum on a case where everything is positive.

lead.text: A cart's velocity climbs steadily while a stopwatch runs.

reveal.text: You divided the change in velocity by the time. Equal time steps add equal velocity changes when the acceleration is constant.

steps.headline: What the sign tells you

lead.text: Velocities have signs, so accelerations do too. The sum uses final minus initial, and it gives the right sign automatically. A cart that slows from 8 m/s to 2 m/s in 3 s changes by 2 − 8 = −6 m/s, so its acceleration is −6 ÷ 3 = −2 m/s². The negative sign is there because the velocity went down.

Now send a cart the other way. A cart that goes from −1 m/s to −9 m/s in 4 s changes by −9 − (−1) = −8 m/s, which gives −8 ÷ 4 = −2 m/s² as well. This time the cart is speeding up, because it moves left faster and faster. The same acceleration slowed the first cart and sped up the second.

afterFigure.text: To tell which one is happening, compare the signs of the velocity and the acceleration. When they match, the acceleration pushes the same way as the motion and the cart speeds up. When they differ, the acceleration works against the motion and the cart slows down. A minus sign on its own does not say whether something is speeding up.

cases.label: Faster to the left: −1 m/s to −9 m/s

steps.headline: A cart moving left goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s in 3 s. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The change in velocity is final minus initial. Subtracting −8 adds 8.
The velocity went up towards zero, so the change is positive.
Divide by the time.

lead.text: Compare the directions of the velocity and the acceleration, rather than reading anything into a minus sign.

steps.headline: Zero acceleration and zero velocity

lead.text: Two mix-ups are worth clearing away. The first is a cart that holds 5 m/s for 3 s. Its velocity does not change, so the change in velocity is 0 and the acceleration is 0 ÷ 3 = 0 m/s². The cart is moving the whole time, yet its acceleration is zero, because acceleration measures how the velocity changes and says nothing about how large the velocity is.

The second is the reverse. Roll a cart up a gentle slope. It slows, stops for an instant at the top and rolls back down. Its velocity passes through +2, +1, 0, −1 and −2 m/s, one step every second, so it changes by −1 m/s each second the whole way. At the instant of stopping, its velocity is zero. Its acceleration is still −1 m/s², because the velocity is in the middle of changing.

afterFigure.text: Velocity and acceleration are separate quantities, and either can be zero while the other is not. The way to find acceleration is the same each time: the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

cases.label: Up the slope and back: 2 m/s to −2 m/s

lead.text: A cart rolls along a flat track without speeding up or slowing down.

reveal.text: Velocity did not change, so acceleration is zero, yet the position keeps changing.

blocks.text: Sit in the front passenger seat of a car at the traffic lights and watch the speedometer. The light turns green and the driver sets off. The needle swings round: first 0, then 3 metres per second, then 6, then 9. It never stays still, because the car's velocity is changing all the time.

Until now every trip we described had a velocity that stayed fixed along each stretch, so one number was enough. The car in the queue needs two. One says how fast it is going, and the other says how quickly that is changing. You feel the second one in your back as the seat pushes you forwards. A gentle start and a hard start can reach the same velocity and feel completely different, because the velocity changed at different rates.
That rate is the subject of this lesson. We'll give it a name and learn to work it out from a trip.

recap.keyIdea: Acceleration is the change in velocity over the time it takes. Its sign comes from final minus initial velocity, and whether something speeds up or slows down depends on how that sign compares with the velocity's.

blocks.text: You found that a car at 10 m/s gaining 3 m/s each second reaches 22 m/s after 4 s. You also saw that a cart going from −8 to −2 m/s has a positive acceleration while it slows, and that a steady velocity means zero acceleration.

lessons.title: Predict the next position

steps.headline: Velocity after a given time

lead.text: Start with the velocity. Say the cart passes the start line at 1 m/s and its acceleration is 3 m/s². An acceleration that stays the same all the way through is called a constant acceleration. The velocity then gains 3 m/s every second: 4 m/s after one second, 7 m/s after two.
Write u for the starting velocity, a for the acceleration and t for the time. The velocity after t seconds is the starting velocity plus the gain per second times the number of seconds.

For t = 2 s that gives 1 + 3 × 2 = 7 m/s. A negative acceleration works the same way. A cart that starts at 9 m/s with a = −2 m/s² has 9 + (−2) × 3 = 3 m/s after 3 s, because each second takes 2 m/s away.

afterFigure.text: The formula tells us how fast the cart is going at the end. How far it has gone is a separate question, and the next few screens deal with it.

lead.text: A cart passes the start line at 3 m/s, and its acceleration stays at 2 m/s² while it runs.

reveal.text: You added the velocity gained each second to the starting velocity: 3 + 2 × 4.

lead.text: The brakes press on, so the acceleration is negative and takes velocity away each second.

steps.headline: Distance at a steady velocity

lead.text: On to the second prediction, the distance. Start with the easy case, a velocity that never changes. A cyclist who holds 6 m/s for 5 s covers 6 × 5 = 30 m. That follows from the definition of average velocity. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, so the displacement is the average velocity times the time.
For a trip of 4 seconds at 6 m/s the answer is 24 m, and twice as long gives twice as far. The distance grows in step with the time whenever the velocity stays fixed.

The same idea carries over when the velocity is not steady, as long as we use the right average. An accelerating cart has a different velocity at every moment, so there is no single obvious number to multiply by. Finding that number is the step after this one.
A train runs along a straight track and its velocity never changes.

steps.headline: Distance when the velocity changes

lead.text: Now let the velocity change. A cart that starts at 1 m/s and speeds up at 2 m/s² for 4 s ends at 1 + 2 × 4 = 9 m/s, using the formula from earlier. Its velocity was 1 m/s at the start and 9 m/s at the end, and it took every value in between along the way. That leaves a puzzle about which velocity to multiply by the time.

With constant acceleration the velocity rises by the same amount every second, so it moves through its values evenly. The time spent slower than the midpoint is matched by the time spent faster, and the two balance out. The average velocity is the mean of the two ends: (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s. Multiply by the 4 s and the cart has gone 5 × 4 = 20 m.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both motions covering the same 20 m, which is why the mean of the ends works. It has a limit. The mean of the start and finish velocities is the average only while the acceleration is constant. The sum also needs the finishing velocity, so you will usually find that first, using the formula from the first screen.

cases.label: Starts at 1 m/s, a = 2 m/s², 4 s

steps.headline: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it go?

workedSteps.text: Find the final velocity from v = u + at.
Average the start and the finish.
Distance is average velocity times time.

steps.headline: Braking to a stop

lead.text: One case turns up often enough to have its own screen: a vehicle braking to a halt. Brakes slow a cart at a steady rate until it stops. The acceleration is constant and negative, and the finishing velocity is 0.

The average of the start and the finish is then half the starting velocity. A cart that brakes from 10 m/s to rest in 5 s has an average velocity of (10 + 0) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s, so it travels 5 × 5 = 25 m before it stops. You do not need to know the acceleration itself. The velocity at each end and the time between them are enough.

afterFigure.text: Real brakes are never perfectly steady, so this is an estimate. For a first look at a stopping distance it is a good one.

lead.text: A cart slows steadily until it stops.

reveal.text: Same method: the average of 12 and 0 is 6 m/s, and that applies for the whole 4 s.

steps.headline: A shortcut and a starting point

lead.text: Putting the pieces together gives a shortcut. The average of u and v = u + at is u + ½at, and multiplying by the time t gives the displacement, which we write s.

Take a cart that starts at 6 m/s with a = 2 m/s² for 3 s. The shortcut gives 6 × 3 + ½ × 2 × 3² = 18 + 9 = 27 m. The two-step method agrees: the cart ends at 12 m/s, averages 9 m/s and goes 9 × 3 = 27 m. The shortcut skips the finishing velocity, but it only holds while the acceleration is constant.
A displacement is a change of position, so to say where the cart ends up you add it to where it began. A cart that starts at the 10 m mark and has a displacement of 27 m finishes at the 37 m mark.

afterFigure.text: From rest, u is 0 and the formula shrinks to s = ½at². The time is squared, so doubling the time makes the cart go four times as far, and tripling it makes the cart go nine times as far. This is why an object that speeds up from rest seems to gather distance faster and faster.

lead.text: A cart starts from rest and speeds up at a constant rate. We only know what it did in its first 2 seconds.

reveal.text: Doubling the time quadruples the distance, so the cart has gone four times 6 m.

blocks.text: A cart rolls along a long straight track, and you stand further down it with a stopwatch. You know how fast the cart was going when it passed the start line, and you know it is speeding up at a steady rate. Before it reaches you, you would like to say how fast it will be going in four seconds' time and how far it will have travelled.
Making that kind of prediction is a main use of physics. From a few facts about the present you work out what an object will do next, with no need to wait and watch.

Everything needed is already in hand. We know that velocity changes at a rate called the acceleration, and we know that velocity and time give displacement. This lesson joins the two into a pair of predictions, one for the velocity after a given time and one for the distance covered.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and the displacement of a cart that accelerates at a constant rate.

recap.keyIdea: With constant acceleration, v = u + at, and displacement is the mean of the start and finish velocities times the time, which gives s = ut + ½at².

blocks.text: You found that a train at 5 m/s covers 40 m in 8 s. You then used the mean of two velocities to find how far a cart travels while it speeds up or brakes, and saw that from rest, doubling the time quadruples the distance.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is a constant acceleration too. Next we drop a ball and see how far it falls.

lessons.title: Falling and rising

steps.headline: A stone speeds up as it falls

lead.text: Let go of a stone and gravity pulls it towards the ground. Film it and measure its velocity, and you find that it picks up the same amount every second: 10 m/s after one second, 30 m/s after three. A steady gain every second is a constant acceleration, as in the last lesson, so gravity gives the stone one.

That acceleration has its own letter, g. Near the Earth's surface it is 9.8 m/s², and this course uses 10 m/s² to keep the sums short unless a question says otherwise. We say an object is in free fall when gravity is the only thing acting on it. That rules out air resistance, the drag of the air on anything moving through it, which is why a leaf drifts down and a stone does not.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a stone dropped from 80 m. Each second it adds another 10 m/s, and after 4 s it hits the ground at 40 m/s. That one steady gain is enough to predict the rest of the fall, starting with how fast the stone is going at any moment.

lead.text: A stone is dropped from the top of a tall cliff and falls freely.

reveal.text: The stone gains 10 m/s every second, so after 5 s it has gained 5 × 10 m/s.

steps.headline: Which way is positive

lead.text: So far the numbers have only said how fast the stone goes. A throw also has a direction. The stone goes up for a while and then comes down, and signs are how we keep track of that. We choose one direction to count as positive, and in this lesson it is up. A height above the starting point is then positive, and so is a velocity that points upward.

Gravity pulls downward, so a stone dropped from rest soon moves downward, and its velocity is negative. After one second it is −10 m/s. Its acceleration is negative too, −10 m/s². The minus sign does not say the stone is slowing down. It says which way the velocity is changing, and here it is changing towards down. With u = 0 and a = −10, the rule from the last lesson gives v = 0 + (−10) × 4 = −40 m/s after 4 s.

afterFigure.text: The graph shows both cases that we meet in this lesson. For the dropped stone the velocity line slopes steadily downward from zero. For a stone thrown upward it starts above zero, falls through zero and carries on below. The slope of a velocity graph is the acceleration, so the two lines have the same slope because the two stones have the same acceleration.

lead.text: A ball is released from rest. Upward is positive.

reveal.text: You used v = u + at with a = −10. A negative velocity means the ball moves downward.

steps.headline: How far the stone has fallen

lead.text: Velocity tells us how fast. The next thing to predict is where the stone is. From the last lesson, the distance covered while speeding up at a steady rate is the average velocity times the time. A stone dropped from rest is going 10t m/s after t seconds, so over those t seconds its average velocity is half of that, 5t m/s. Multiplying by the time gives a distance fallen of 5t × t = 5t². In symbols that is ½gt², which is ½ × 10 × t².

After 1 s the stone has fallen 5 m. After 4 s it has fallen 5 × 4² = 80 m, sixteen times as far in a time only four times as long. Time is squared, so a fall that lasts twice as long covers four times the distance. In the picture a stone dropped from 80 m reaches the ground at exactly 4 s.

afterFigure.text: A distance fallen is not yet a height. With up as positive, the fall is a displacement of −½gt², and the height is where the stone started plus that displacement: height = starting height − ½gt². A stone dropped from 80 m is 5 m lower after 1 s, so it is at 75 m.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 80 m. How high is it after 3 s?

workedSteps.text: The distance fallen is ½gt².
The ball moves down, so its displacement is negative.
Add the displacement to the starting height.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 45 m. How high is it after 2 s?

workedSteps.text: The distance fallen in 2 s is ½gt².
Take that fall off the starting height of 45 m.

steps.headline: A stone thrown upward

lead.text: Now throw the stone straight up at 20 m/s. Gravity does not wait for the stone to start falling. It pulls down from the instant the stone leaves your hand, so the upward velocity shrinks by 10 m/s every second. It is 10 m/s after one second and zero after two. For an instant the stone is not moving at all, and that instant is the top of the throw. Afterwards its velocity is negative because it is heading down, and 2 s after the top it is back at your hand, moving at −20 m/s.

Look at what stays the same. The velocity goes from positive through zero to negative, but the acceleration is −10 m/s² all the way: on the way up, at the top and on the way down. A velocity of zero does not mean an acceleration of zero. At the top the velocity is changing as fast as at any other moment, and it is simply passing through zero on its way from up to down.

afterFigure.text: The height of a throw follows the same rule as before with the starting velocity u added in: displacement = ut − ½gt². For this stone at 2 s that is 20 × 2 − 5 × 2² = 20 m, so the top of the throw is 20 m above your hand. At 4 s it is 20 × 4 − 5 × 4² = 0, back where it started.

lead.text: Throw a ball straight up. It slows, stops for an instant at the top, then drops back.

reveal.text: The velocity is zero at the top but the acceleration is not. Gravity gave −10 on the way up and gives −10 now.

steps.headline: Does a heavy stone fall faster

lead.text: One question is left from the start of the lesson, whether a heavy stone falls faster than a light one. It seems obvious that it does, and a hammer and a feather dropped together seem to prove it. The picture is misleading because of the air. The feather catches the air and the hammer hardly does. In free fall nothing but gravity is acting, so there is no such difference to blame.

A heavy stone has more mass, the amount of matter in it, measured in kilograms. The acceleration we have used all lesson never mentioned mass, and that is the answer. Gravity does pull harder on a stone of larger mass, but the larger stone also has more matter to get moving. The two effects cancel exactly, so a 2 kg ball and an 8 kg ball let go together stay level all the way down.

afterFigure.text: In 1971 an astronaut on the Moon, where there is no air, dropped a hammer and a feather together. They reached the ground at the same moment.

lead.text: Two balls of different mass leave the same height at the same moment. Air resistance is ignored.

reveal.text: Mass cancels: a heavier ball is pulled harder but also has more to move. Free fall is the same for both.

lessons.orientation: Apply constant downward acceleration to free fall and an upward throw.

blocks.text: Hold a stone out over the edge of a high bridge and let go. For the first instant it hardly seems to move. A moment later it is dropping quickly, and by the time it reaches the river you can barely follow it. Throw the same stone straight up and it does something just as odd. It climbs, slows, hangs for a moment at the top and then comes back down.

The last lesson ended with a way to predict where a cart will be when it speeds up at a steady rate. Gravity turns out to be a steady rate too, so the same sums describe the stone on its way down, on its way up and in the instant between.

We follow one stone. We drop it and work out how fast it goes and how far it falls, then throw it upward and watch what gravity does at the top. The last stop is an old argument, whether a heavy stone falls faster than a light one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and height of a falling or thrown ball, and say what gravity does at the top.

recap.keyIdea: Free fall has one constant acceleration, 10 m/s² downward, whether the object rises, falls or sits at the top. Mass does not change it.

blocks.text: You worked out that a stone is going 50 m/s after falling for 5 s, and that a ball dropped from 45 m is 25 m up after 2 s. You also saw that a ball thrown upward has an acceleration of −10 m/s² at its highest point, where its velocity is zero.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is seldom the only pull on an object. Next we add up several pushes and pulls and see what they do together.

lessons.title: When forces balance

steps.headline: Putting numbers on a pull

lead.text: To put numbers on the rope we need a unit. A push or a pull on an object is called a force, and forces are measured in newtons, written N. One newton is roughly the pull of gravity on a small apple, so the pull of a tug-of-war team, a few hundred newtons, is a strong one. Suppose the left team pulls with 400 N and the right team with 350 N.

A force has a direction as well as a size, and we draw it as an arrow that points the way it pulls. The two teams' arrows lie along the same rope and point opposite ways, so they work against each other. The smaller pull takes away part of the larger one, and what is left over decides which way the flag slides. The left team wins, and the size of its lead is the amount the two pulls leave over.
Think of the rope as the object. Two arrows act on it, one in each direction.

reveal.text: The smaller pull cancels part of the larger one, so the lead is 400 − 350 newtons.

steps.headline: Adding forces with signs

lead.text: The leftover in the tug of war has a name. It is the net force on the rope, the combined effect of every force acting on it. To find the net force on any object, first decide which object you mean, because only the forces acting on that object count. Then choose a direction to count as positive. Say it is right. A force pointing right gets a plus sign and a force pointing left gets a minus sign.

For the rope, the right team gives +350 N and the left team gives −400 N. Added together they make −50 N, which is the answer to the last question with a direction attached. The size, 50 N, says how much is left over, and the minus sign says the leftover points left, so the flag slides towards the stronger team.

afterFigure.text: The same rule works for any number of forces. Give each force its sign and add them all. A plus sign on the result means the net force points the way you chose as positive, and a minus sign means it points the other way.

lead.text: Two horizontal forces act on a cart. One points right and one points left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You gave the leftward force a minus sign and added: 14 − 6. The sum points right, so it is positive.

steps.headline: A sled has forces of 12 N right, 7 N left and 3 N left. Find the net force.

workedSteps.text: Give each force its sign, rightward positive.
Add them.
The result is small and positive, so the sled's net push is slightly to the right.

steps.headline: A resting cart has 9 N right and 9 N left on it. What is the net force?

workedSteps.text: The rightward force counts as positive.
The leftward force counts as negative.
Add them.

steps.headline: What a net force of zero does

lead.text: The last example had a cart with 9 N pulling one way and 9 N pulling the other, and the sum came to zero. When the net force on an object is zero we say the forces on it are balanced. Their effects cancel, and the object behaves as if nothing were acting on it.

For an object at rest that is easy to accept, since a book on a table stays where it is. The surprise is what happens to something already moving. A cart rolling at 5 m/s with balanced forces on it carries on at 5 m/s, in the same direction, for as long as the forces stay balanced. Nothing has to keep pushing it.

afterFigure.text: Everyday life seems to say otherwise, because a ball rolling over grass slows and stops. The reason is a second force that we left out, friction, the rubbing of the grass against the ball. The forces on the ball are no longer balanced, which is why its velocity changes. A puck on smooth ice has very little friction and slides a long way at nearly the same speed. The rule that balanced forces leave the velocity unchanged is called Newton's first law of motion.

cases.label: Rolling at 5 m/s, 12 N each way

lead.text: A cart rolls right at 3 m/s. The forces on it add up to zero.

reveal.text: Zero net force means no change in velocity, so the cart keeps its 3 m/s. It needs no push to keep going.

steps.headline: A force that points against the motion

lead.text: Now unbalance the forces. A cart is rolling to the right, and the net force on it points left. A force says nothing about where an object is going. It says how the velocity changes. A leftward net force pushes the velocity towards the left, so the cart's rightward velocity shrinks. The cart slows, stops for an instant and, if the force keeps acting, starts to move left.

The direction of the net force and the direction of the motion are separate things. When they agree, the object speeds up. When they point opposite ways, it slows down. That matches what you found about speeding up and slowing down in the lesson on changing velocity, and it adds where the change comes from: a net force.
A cart rolls right, but the bigger force on it points left.

reveal.text: The net force points left while the cart still moves right. The force changes the velocity; it does not show where the cart is going.

lessons.orientation: Add signed forces and distinguish balanced forces from being at rest.

blocks.text: Two teams take hold of a rope. One team pulls to the left as hard as it can and the other pulls to the right. A flag tied to the middle of the rope hangs over a line painted on the grass, and everyone watches the flag. For a while it hardly moves. Then, slowly, it begins to slide towards one side.

In the last lesson the stone had only one pull on it, from gravity, so we only had to ask how that single pull changed its motion. Almost everything else around you has several pushes and pulls on it at once. A book on a table and a swimmer in a pool both do, and what each one does depends on how its pushes and pulls add up.

This lesson follows the rope. We put numbers on the pulls and add them, then find out what an object does when they cancel exactly, which is less obvious than it sounds. We finish with a cart that is rolling one way while the bigger pull on it points the other way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add up the pushes and pulls on an object, and say what happens to its velocity when they cancel.

recap.keyIdea: The net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object. When it is zero, the velocity does not change.

blocks.text: You found that a 400 N pull and a 350 N pull leave 50 N over, and that a cart with balanced forces keeps rolling at 3 m/s. You also met a net force of −12 N acting on a cart that was still moving to the right.

recap.nextHook: A net force of zero leaves the velocity alone. Next we find out how much the velocity changes when the net force is not zero.

lessons.title: Force, mass and acceleration

steps.headline: The empty trolley and the loaded one

lead.text: Take a supermarket trolley of mass 5 kg and push it with a steady 10 N. Its velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, so its acceleration is 2 m/s². Now load it until its mass is 10 kg, which is twice as much. Push with the same 10 N and the loaded trolley is harder to get moving. Its velocity rises by only 1 m/s every second. Doubling the mass halved the acceleration.

Go back to the empty trolley and push twice as hard, with 20 N. Now it speeds up by 4 m/s every second, so doubling the push doubled the acceleration. The direction matters too. The trolley speeds up the way you push, so the acceleration points the way the force points.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares the three trolleys. Two patterns show in it. The acceleration grows in step with the force and shrinks in step with the mass. The next screen turns both into a single rule.

lead.text: Loading the trolley changes its mass and leaves the push alone.

reveal.text: Twice the mass with the same push gives half the acceleration, so 6 ÷ 2.

steps.headline: Newton's second law

lead.text: Both patterns fit a single rule: the acceleration equals the net force divided by the mass. This is Newton's second law of motion. In symbols it is a = F ÷ m, where F is the net force, m is the mass and a is the acceleration. It is more often written F = ma, which says the same thing.

The rule is also where the newton comes from. A net force of 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². The 5 kg trolley fits: 10 N ÷ 5 kg = 2 m/s². The rule needs the net force, so when several forces act on an object they are first added with their signs, and only the total is divided by the mass. A positive net force gives a positive acceleration. A net force of zero gives an acceleration of zero, which is the balanced case from the last lesson.
A 3 kg cart has two horizontal forces on it, one pointing right and one pointing left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You found the net force first, then divided by the mass. That is the second law at work.

steps.headline: A trolley of mass 8 kg has 30 N right and 6 N left on it. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: Find the net force. The leftward force is negative.
Divide the net force by the mass.
The sign is positive, so the acceleration points right.

steps.headline: A net force of 24 N pushes a 2 kg cart to the right. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The force given is already the net force.
The mass is 2 kg.
Divide the net force by the mass.

steps.headline: The acceleration follows the net force

lead.text: The rule says nothing about which way the object is moving, only about the net force on it. Take a 2 kg cart rolling to the right at 5 m/s, with a 10 N force acting to the left. The net force is −10 N, so the acceleration is −10 ÷ 2 = −5 m/s². The cart is still moving right, but each second its velocity falls by 5 m/s. After one second it is stationary, and after that it starts to move left.

This is the pattern from the lesson on changing velocity, and now we can say what causes it. If the velocity and the net force point the same way, the object speeds up. If they point opposite ways it slows down, and if the force keeps acting it eventually reverses. Braking is the everyday case: the net force on the car points backwards while the car moves forwards.
A 4 kg cart moves right at 6 m/s. A 4 N force pushes it right and a 12 N force pushes it left.

reveal.text: The acceleration follows the net force. The cart is still going right, and it is slowing down.

steps.headline: Finding the force or the mass

lead.text: The rule can be turned round. Sometimes the acceleration is known and the force is what we want. A 5 kg trolley that has to speed up at 3 m/s² needs a net force of F = ma = 5 × 3 = 15 N.

Sometimes the force and the acceleration are known and the mass is the unknown. Dividing both sides of F = ma by a gives m = F ÷ a. A net force of 30 N that produces an acceleration of 6 m/s² is acting on a mass of 30 ÷ 6 = 5 kg. Pushing something and watching how fast it speeds up is a way to find its mass without putting it on a scale.

The rule also compares objects. For the same acceleration, a larger mass needs a larger net force, because F = ma grows with m. Pushing a loaded trolley up to the same acceleration as an empty one takes more effort.
Now the other way round: the mass and the acceleration are known, and the net force is not.

reveal.text: Net force is mass times acceleration, so the force is 4 × 3 newtons.

lessons.orientation: Use net force and mass to predict how velocity changes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You push an empty supermarket trolley across a car park. It gets going quickly, and a few seconds later you are walking briskly beside it. Now load it with a week's shopping and push just as hard. It gets going more slowly. Ask a friend to push alongside you, and it speeds up faster again.

You have felt this many times, and each time it says something about the trolley's acceleration, the rate at which its velocity changes. A bigger push gives more acceleration and a bigger load gives less. The last lesson showed what happens when the pushes and pulls on an object cancel. This one is about what happens when they do not.

We start with the trolley and turn the feeling into a short rule with numbers. Then we use the rule to find an acceleration from a push and to follow a cart that is slowing down. The last step works backwards from an acceleration to the force or the mass behind it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use net force and mass to find acceleration, and work the other way to find a force or a mass.

recap.keyIdea: The net force equals mass times acceleration: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less. The acceleration points the way the net force points.

blocks.text: You saw the same push on twice the mass give half the acceleration, 3 m/s² instead of 6. You found that a cart moving right can accelerate to the left when the net force points that way, and that a net force of 12 N gives a 4 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s².

lessons.title: Weight and support

steps.headline: The pull of gravity on a bag

lead.text: Start with the bag on its own. Gravity pulls on every kilogram of it with a force of about 10 N, so a 2 kg bag is pulled down with 20 N and a 5 kg bag with 50 N. The pull of gravity on an object is called its weight. It grows in step with the mass, so the weight is the mass times the pull on one kilogram.

Here g is 10 N for every kilogram, which is the same number as the 10 m/s² of free fall, because 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons and it points down. Mass is measured in kilograms.

afterFigure.text: This also explains the end of the lesson on falling. A freely falling object has only its weight acting on it, so the second law gives it an acceleration of W ÷ m = mg ÷ m = g. The mass cancels, and every object in free fall has the same acceleration.

lead.text: Each kilogram of the bag is pulled down by the same amount.

steps.headline: What holds the bag up

lead.text: Put the 5 kg bag on a table. Its weight is still 50 N, pulling down. If that were the only force on it, the net force would point down and the bag would accelerate down through the table. It does not, so something is pushing up. The table is, and the upward push of a surface on whatever rests on it is called the support force.

The bag is at rest. Its acceleration is zero, and by the second law the net force on it is zero as well. The upward support force and the downward weight have to be equal and opposite, which means the support force is mg. For the 5 kg bag that is 50 N. The table does not push with a fixed amount. It pushes as hard as it needs to until it breaks, and a heavier bag gets a harder push.

afterFigure.text: Take the table away and the support force goes with it. The weight is then the only force on the bag, which is free fall again.

lead.text: A shelf holds a box in the same way that the table held the bag.

steps.headline: Support in a lift that speeds up

lead.text: Now put the bag in a lift that is speeding up as it rises. The bag accelerates upward with the lift, so its acceleration is not zero and the net force on it cannot be zero either. The second law gives the size of that net force: the mass times the acceleration, pointing up.

Take up as positive. The support force pushes up and the weight pulls down, so the net force is the support force − mg. Setting that equal to ma gives the support force − mg = ma, and so the support force = m(g + a). The floor has to carry the weight and also supply the extra push ma that accelerates the bag. A 3 kg bag in a lift speeding up at 1 m/s² needs 3 × (10 + 1) = 33 N from the floor, which is 3 N more than at rest.

afterFigure.text: That extra push is why you feel heavier for the first moment of a ride up. The floor pushes harder on your feet than it does when the lift is standing still.

cases.label: 3 kg bag, lift speeding up at 1

steps.headline: A 2 kg load is carried upward at 3 m/s² in a lift. Find the support force. Take g as 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The weight is mg.
The net upward force must give the acceleration.
The support force carries the weight and supplies the net force.

steps.headline: A 4 kg object is accelerated upward at 2 m/s². Find the support force with g = 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The weight is mg.
The extra force for the acceleration is ma.
Add them to find the support force.

steps.headline: Lifts that go down or move steadily

lead.text: Turn the lift round and the same equation still works. Only the sign of the acceleration changes. If the lift speeds up downward, a is negative, so m(g + a) is smaller than the weight. A 3 kg bag in a lift speeding up downward at 1 m/s² has a support force of 3 × (10 − 1) = 27 N. The floor pushes less hard, and the bag feels lighter.

What matters is the acceleration, and the direction of travel makes no difference. A lift going down at a steady 2 m/s has an acceleration of zero, so the support force equals the weight, as if the lift were standing still. The same holds for a lift going up at a steady speed. The support force differs from the weight only while the velocity is changing.

Push the idea to its limit. If a is −g, the equation gives zero. The floor stops pushing, and the bag falls freely with the lift. That is the weightless feeling of free fall, and it is what astronauts in orbit feel, since they are falling freely all the time.

steps.headline: Mass stays the same and weight does not

lead.text: Carry the bag to the Moon. Gravity there pulls on each kilogram with about 1.6 N, so g on the Moon is 1.6 N per kilogram against Earth's 10. The 5 kg bag weighs 5 × 1.6 = 8 N and is far easier to lift. It is the same bag with the same amount of matter in it, and its mass is still 5 kg.

Weight and mass are easy to mix up, because everyday language uses both for how heavy something is and on Earth they go together. They are different quantities. Mass, in kilograms, belongs to the object and is the same everywhere. Weight, in newtons, depends on the mass and on g, so it changes from place to place. The second law uses mass, which is why the bag is just as hard to start moving sideways on the Moon as on Earth.
Another planet has a different g from Earth's.

blocks.text: Hold a bag of shopping at arm's length and your arm soon starts to ache. Put the bag on a table and the ache goes, though gravity is pulling on the bag exactly as before. The table is doing the job your arm was doing. The bag is not accelerating in either case, and the second law says what that means: the forces on it add up to zero, so something must be pushing up as hard as gravity pulls down.

Step into a lift with the bag and the story changes. When the lift sets off upward the bag feels heavier, and as the lift slows to a stop at the top it feels lighter. Your arm is a good instrument here, because it tells you how hard the bag has to be held up.
This lesson follows the bag. We put a number on the pull of gravity and work out what holds the bag up when everything is still. Then we see how the answer changes in a lift and on another world.

lessons.title: Forces come in pairs

steps.headline: A push always has a push back

lead.text: Go back to the skaters. When the first skater pushes, she exerts a force on the second skater. At the same moment the second skater exerts a force on her, of the same size and in the opposite direction. If she pushes with 25 N, he pushes back on her with 25 N. The second force is easy to miss because he does not seem to be doing anything, but it is what sends her backwards.

This is Newton's third law of motion. When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts a force on A that is equal in size and opposite in direction. The two forces form a pair, and every force has a partner of this kind. You feel the partner whenever you push on something: a heavy door pushes back against your hand.
A and B are two skaters on smooth ice.

reveal.text: A push and its push back are the same size, so B pushes on A with 40 N.

steps.headline: The two forces act on different objects

lead.text: The forces in a pair are equal and opposite, so you might expect them to cancel. They do not, because they act on different objects. A's push acts on B and B's push acts on A. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object and we add them to find that object's net force. A force on A and a force on B never go into the same sum.
Signs record the opposite directions. Take right as positive. If A pushes B with +30 N, B pushes A with −30 N. The sizes match and the signs differ.

It is easy to mistake two forces on the same object for a pair. A book rests on a table. The weight pulls down on the book and the support force pushes up on the book. They can be equal and opposite, but both act on the book, so they are not a pair. The partner of the table's push up on the book is the book's push down on the table, and the partner of the book's weight is the book's own pull on the Earth.
Carts A and B sit on a track with A on the left.

steps.headline: Equal forces, different accelerations

lead.text: Now ask what each skater does. The two forces are equal, but each acts on its own skater, so we apply the second law to each skater separately. A skater of mass m pushed with a force F accelerates at F ÷ m. Suppose two skaters push each other with 90 N and their masses are 30 kg and 45 kg. Their accelerations are 90 ÷ 30 = 3 m/s² and 90 ÷ 45 = 2 m/s².

The directions are opposite because the forces are. With right as positive, the 30 kg skater is pushed to the left and accelerates at −3 m/s². The 45 kg skater is pushed to the right and accelerates at +2 m/s².

afterFigure.text: The lighter skater gains velocity faster and moves off faster. A pair of equal forces does not give equal motion, because the second law divides each force by the mass of the object it acts on.

steps.headline: Treating both objects as one system

lead.text: Sometimes it helps to draw a boundary round both objects and treat them as a single system. The pair of forces between the skaters is then inside the system. Add up the forces on the system and the pair cancels, because +F from one skater and −F from the other make zero. The pair cannot change the motion of the system as a whole, in the way that two people in a boat cannot move the boat by pushing on each other.

Each skater still accelerates, because each one has an unbalanced force acting on them. The cancelling happens only when both are counted together. To move the system as a whole, something outside it has to push, such as a third skater.

blocks.text: Two skaters stand face to face on smooth ice, both at rest. One of them puts her hands on the other's shoulders and pushes. The skater who was pushed glides backwards, which is what you would expect. The skater who did the pushing glides backwards too, in the opposite direction, although nobody pushed her.

A push on a wall does the same. Lean on a wall while standing on a skateboard and you roll away from it. The wall seems to do nothing, yet it must be pushing on you, because your velocity changed and the second law says that takes a net force.

This lesson looks at that second push, the one you do not see. We find out how big it is, which object it acts on and what it does to each skater. The last step treats the two skaters as one thing, to see what the pushes between them can and cannot do.

lessons.title: Friction that adjusts

steps.headline: Friction that matches your push

lead.text: Start with the crate at rest on a level floor and push on it gently. Nothing moves, and the earlier lessons tell us what that means: an object that is not accelerating has no net force on it. Your push is one force along the floor, so another force along the floor must be cancelling it exactly. That force is friction, which acts along the touching surfaces and opposes any sliding, or any attempt to slide.

Friction between surfaces that are not sliding is called static friction. Push with 10 N and the floor pushes back with 10 N. Push with 18 N and it pushes back with 18 N. It does not keep a fixed amount in reserve. It supplies whatever is needed to hold the crate still, which is why it can seem to know how hard you are pushing.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a 4 kg box pushed with 12 N and then with 18 N. In both cases the box stays where it is, and the friction arrow is exactly as long as the push. That raises the question of how far this can go, because a floor cannot go on matching a bigger and bigger push for ever.

lead.text: A crate that stays at rest is not accelerating.

reveal.text: The crate is not accelerating, so the net force on it is zero. Friction cancels your push exactly, which makes it 30 N.

steps.headline: The most static friction can hold

lead.text: Now keep increasing the push. For a while the friction keeps up. Then there comes a push it cannot match: the crate gives way and starts to slide. So static friction has a ceiling, and a push above the ceiling wins.

Two things set the ceiling. The first is how hard the two surfaces are pressed together. On a level floor that is the support force, which you met in the lesson on weight and which equals mg when nothing else pushes up or down. A heavier crate is pressed down harder and grips harder. The second is the pair of surfaces. Rubber on dry concrete grips far better than steel on ice. A number called the coefficient of friction records this, and for static friction it is written μs.

Take a 10 kg crate on a floor where μs = 0.4, with g = 10 m/s². The support force is 10 × 10 = 100 N, so the ceiling is 0.4 × 100 = 40 N. Any push up to 40 N is matched exactly. A push of 45 N is not, and the crate slides.

steps.headline: A 3 kg crate has μs = 0.4. It is pushed with 15 N on a level floor. Does it slide? Use g = 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: On a level floor the support force equals the weight.
The most static friction the floor can give.
The 15 N push beats the 12 N limit, so the crate slides.

steps.headline: A 4 kg box has μs = 0.5. What is the most static friction it can get, with g = 10 m/s²?

workedSteps.text: The support force equals the weight.
Multiply by the coefficient of static friction.

lead.text: A 4 kg box on this floor can hold at most 20 N of static friction. You push it with 12 N and it stays put.

reveal.text: Friction matched your push, 12 N. The 20 N is only the ceiling, not what friction supplies.

steps.headline: Friction on a sliding box

lead.text: Suppose the push has beaten the ceiling and the crate is moving. Anyone who has shifted furniture knows what comes next: it gets easier. Once two surfaces slide over each other, the friction between them drops to a smaller value, called sliding friction.

Sliding friction is found the same way as the ceiling, with a different coefficient. The coefficient for sliding is written μk, and for the same two surfaces it is smaller than μs. Take a 5 kg box with μs = 0.5 and μk = 0.3. Its support force is 5 × 10 = 50 N. The ceiling is 0.5 × 50 = 25 N, but once the box is sliding the friction is 0.3 × 50 = 15 N.

afterFigure.text: Sliding friction also differs from static friction in that it does not depend on the push. The picture shows the box sliding while it is pushed with 30 N and then with 20 N. The friction arrow is the same length both times. A harder push changes how quickly the box speeds up. The friction stays the same.

lead.text: The box now slides. Use the sliding coefficient this time. The support force is still mg.

reveal.text: Sliding friction is fixed by the coefficient and the support force. It does not grow with the push.

steps.headline: How a sliding box speeds up

lead.text: With sliding friction fixed, we can say how a sliding box moves. Two forces act along the floor: your push and the friction against it. With right positive, the friction is negative and the net force is the push minus the friction. The second law then gives the acceleration, the net force divided by the mass. Take a 6 kg box with sliding friction of 18 N, pushed right with 30 N. The net force is 30 − 18 = 12 N and the acceleration is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s².

Other cases follow from the same sum. If the push equals the friction, the net force is zero and the box slides at a steady speed. If you take the push away altogether, only friction is left. It points against the motion, so the box slows down.

afterFigure.text: When the box stops, the friction stops too. Friction opposes sliding, or an attempt to slide. With the box at rest and nothing pushing it, there is nothing for friction to oppose, so it falls to zero. It cannot start the box moving backwards.

lead.text: A sliding 4 kg box is pushed right with 24 N while sliding friction pulls left.

reveal.text: Net force is push minus friction. That is what accelerates the box: 12 N on 4 kg.

blocks.text: Try pushing a heavy crate across a floor. You lean in and nothing happens. You push harder and it still does not move. Then, at some point, it gives way and slides, and from then on it takes less effort to keep it going than it did to get it started.

The floor has been pushing back the whole time. The last lesson showed a table pushing up on a book, and the floor pushes up on the crate in the same way. Because the surfaces are rough it also pushes along the floor, against your push. That force is friction. It is not one fixed amount. It changes as you push harder, and it changes again the moment the crate starts to move.

This lesson follows one crate while the push grows from nothing. We find how much friction holds the crate still and where its limit lies. Then we see what changes once the crate is moving, and use the numbers to find how quickly a sliding crate speeds up.

recap.keyIdea: Static friction matches the push up to a limit of μs times the support force. Sliding friction is μk times that, and the net force comes from push minus friction.

blocks.text: You found that friction cancelled a 30 N push on a crate that did not move, and that a 15 N push beats a 12 N limit. For a 4 kg box you found a limit of 20 N, sliding friction of 12 N and an acceleration of 3 m/s² under a 24 N push.

recap.nextHook: Friction took 12 N from the push in that last example, and what was left still moved the box. Next we measure what a force achieves when it moves something over a distance.

lessons.title: When a force does work

steps.headline: Counting the effort of a push

lead.text: Push a box along a floor with a steady force and keep a tally of the effort as you go. Suppose a push of 10 N moves the box 3 m. Each metre costs the same, because the push is steady, so the total is the cost of one metre times the number of metres. Call the cost of pushing 10 N over one metre 10 units. Then 3 m costs 30 units.

The size of the push matters in the same way. Push twice as hard over the same 3 m, with 20 N, and every metre costs twice as much, so the total is 60 units. Doubling the distance doubles the tally, and doubling the force doubles it too. A tally that behaves like this is a product: the force multiplied by the distance moved. The next screen gives that product a name.
Each metre of a steady push costs the same amount.

reveal.text: Each metre costs 10 units, so eight metres cost eight times that.

steps.headline: Force times distance, in joules

lead.text: Physicists call this product work. When a steady force acts in the direction an object moves, the work it does is the force times the distance moved.
The unit is the joule, written J. One joule is the work done by a force of 1 N over 1 m. A 10 N push over 3 m does 30 J, and the units in our tally were joules all along.

The word has a narrow meaning. A force does work only while the object it acts on moves along it. Hold a bag at arm's length and your arm pushes up on it, but the bag does not move, so that force does no work on it. Your muscles still tire, because they are straining, but that cost is inside your body and does not count as work on the bag.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the same 12 N force acts over 3 m and then over 6 m. Doubling the distance doubles the work, from 36 J to 72 J.

lead.text: A constant 15 N force acts in the same direction as a 4 m move of the object it pushes.

reveal.text: You multiplied force by distance, so the work is positive: the force acts along the move.

steps.headline: Forces that oppose the move

lead.text: So far the force and the move pointed the same way. Often they do not. A box sliding across a floor is pushed along, but friction pulls on it the other way. Friction acts against the move, and the work it does is negative. Negative work means the force is taking something away from the movement and not adding to it.

The size is still force times distance, and the sign records which way the force points compared with the move. A box slides 4 m while 5 N of friction acts against it. The friction does −5 × 4 = −20 J of work. A force along the move does positive work and a force against it does negative work.

steps.headline: A box slides 3 m while an 8 N friction force acts against it. Find the work done by friction.

workedSteps.text: Friction points against the displacement, so its work is negative.
Multiply force by distance.
Attach the sign.

steps.headline: A 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its work.

workedSteps.text: The force opposes the move, so the work is negative.
Multiply the force by the distance, with the sign.

steps.headline: Forces at right angles to the move

lead.text: A third case sits between the first two. Carry a tray of drinks across a room at a steady pace. Your hands push up on the tray while the tray moves sideways. The upward force is at right angles to the move, and it does no work, because it neither pushes the tray further along nor holds it back.

Only the part of a force that points along the move counts. A force at right angles has no part along the move, so its work is zero. The support force from a floor does no work on a box sliding across it, for the same reason. A 30 N support force acting while a box moves 5 m does 0 J of work.
A vertical support force acts while the box slides horizontally.

reveal.text: The support force has no part along the move, so its work is zero.

steps.headline: Several forces on one object

lead.text: A real object usually has several forces on it, and each one does its own work. To find the work of one force, use only that force and the move. A cart is pulled 4 m with 30 N while 10 N of friction acts against it. The pull does 30 × 4 = 120 J, and the friction does −10 × 4 = −40 J.

Adding the works with their signs gives the net work: 120 − 40 = 80 J. This agrees with the net force times the distance, since the net force is 30 − 10 = 20 N and 20 × 4 = 80 J. Positive net work means the forces together are helping the move along, and negative net work means they are holding it back.
Several forces may act on a cart. The work of each is found separately, from that force and the move.

reveal.text: This pull does 70 J. A separate opposing 4 N force over the same 7 m would do −28 J.

blocks.text: Push a heavy box across a room and you feel it. A short shove is easy. A long push is tiring, and a harder push tires you faster. Now hold a heavy bag at arm's length for a minute. Your arm shakes and you are worn out, yet the bag has not moved at all.

Tiredness is a poor measure, because it depends on the person and on how long they take. Physics wants a number that depends only on the push and the move, so that anyone can calculate it and two people can compare. The last lesson ended with a box sliding along against friction, with part of the push used up. That is a good place to start counting.

We begin with a tally of the effort in a steady push and turn it into a rule with a unit. Then we see what happens when the force points against the move or across it, and what to do when several forces act at once. The bag at arm's length gets an answer on the way.
