lessons.title: Energy of motion

steps.headline: What the brakes take away

lead.text: Brakes press on the wheel and produce a force against the bike's motion. That force acts over the stopping distance, so it does negative work on the bike: the braking force times the distance, with a minus sign. By the time the bike has stopped, the brakes have removed everything it had because it was moving.

That quantity needs a name. It is called kinetic energy, the amount an object holds because of its motion. We can measure it by asking how much work it takes to bring the object to rest, and it is counted in joules, like work. A bike at rest has none, and a faster bike has more.

With a steady braking force, the kinetic energy equals the braking force times the stopping distance. For the same brakes, a bike with more kinetic energy has to travel further before it stops. What remains is to find how the kinetic energy depends on the bike's mass and speed.

steps.headline: Kinetic energy is ½mv²

lead.text: Take a 3 kg cart rolling at 2 m/s and brake it with a steady 3 N. The second law gives an acceleration of 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m/s² against the motion, so the cart stops after 2 s. Its speed falls steadily from 2 m/s to 0, which makes its average speed 1 m/s, so it travels 1 × 2 = 2 m. The brakes do 3 × 2 = 6 J of work. The cart began with 6 J of kinetic energy.

Doing the same sum with letters gives the general rule. A mass m at speed v is braked by a steady force F. Its acceleration is a = F ÷ m, it stops in a time v ÷ a, and it covers the average speed, v ÷ 2, times that time. The work F times that distance simplifies, using F = ma, to half the mass times the speed squared.

afterFigure.text: Check the cart against the formula: ½ × 3 × 2² = 6 J. The speed is squared and the mass is not, and that difference decides almost everything that follows. Kinetic energy is never negative, and it does not depend on which way the object moves.

lead.text: For the same brakes, the stopping distance is the kinetic energy divided by the braking force.

reveal.text: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy to remove, so the stopping distance is four times as long.

lead.text: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Use the formula from the last screen.

reveal.text: You squared the speed, multiplied by the mass and halved it: ½ × 2 × 9 gives 9 J.

steps.headline: A 1 kg ball speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Compare its kinetic energies.

workedSteps.text: Kinetic energy at 2 m/s.
Kinetic energy at 4 m/s.
Divide the new energy by the old.

workedSteps.text: Mass is fixed, so only v² can change.
Replace v with 2v and square it.

steps.headline: Why speed counts for more than mass

lead.text: The squared speed has consequences you can feel on the road. A car at 60 km/h has four times the kinetic energy of the same car at 30 km/h. Its brakes have to remove four times as much, and with the same braking force it needs four times the distance. A modest drop in speed shortens the stopping distance by a lot, which is why speed limits near schools are low.

Mass enters the formula once, so it has a gentler effect. A loaded lorry and an empty one at the same speed differ in kinetic energy in proportion to their masses, and the loaded one needs more from its brakes. Both matter, but doubling the speed does far more than doubling the mass.

steps.headline: Net work changes kinetic energy

lead.text: Braking is one case of a general rule. The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy, the final value minus the initial value.

A 5 kg trolley speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Its kinetic energy rises from ½ × 5 × 2² = 10 J to ½ × 5 × 4² = 40 J, so the net work done on it is 40 − 10 = +30 J. Let it slow from 4 m/s back to 2 m/s and the net work is −30 J. Positive net work speeds an object up and negative net work slows it down. A bike that brakes to rest loses all its kinetic energy, so the net work on it is minus its starting kinetic energy.
A 2 kg cart is pushed until it goes faster. Find the energy at each speed first.

reveal.text: Net work is the gain in kinetic energy, from 9 J to 25 J.

lead.text: Keep the speed fixed and change the mass instead.

reveal.text: Mass enters ½mv² once, so energy scales with mass directly. Speed is the term that is squared.

The bike does not stop in twice the distance. It runs on much further than that, which is why a fast car needs so much more room than a slow one.

The last lesson gave us a way to count what a force does as it acts over a distance. Brakes are a force acting over a distance, and they finish with the bike at rest. So the work the brakes do must be tied to how fast the bike was going, and that link should explain the surprise.

We start from the brakes and find what a moving object has that they remove. Then we write it as a formula, use the formula to follow the bike at two speeds, and say what the net work on any object changes about its motion.

lessons.title: Energy and height

steps.headline: The work of a slow lift

lead.text: Start with the lift. Raise a 6 kg bag at a steady speed onto a shelf 1.5 m up, taking g = 10 m/s². A steady speed means no acceleration, so the net force on the bag is zero and your upward pull must equal its weight: mg = 6 × 10 = 60 N.

Your pull points along the move, so it does work equal to the force times the height: 60 × 1.5 = 90 J. A bag twice as heavy takes twice the force, and a shelf twice as high takes twice the distance. For a slow lift through a height h the work is mg × h, and it does not depend on how long the lift takes.
You lift a 4 kg box slowly onto a shelf 2 m higher.

reveal.text: The lift is steady, so the force matches the weight. The work is 40 × 2 = 80 J.

steps.headline: Height stores energy

lead.text: Where did the 90 J go? The bag is not moving, so it is not kinetic energy. The bag is simply higher, and the guess from the start says the height holds it. Release the bag and it falls, gravity does work on it, and if air resistance is small it reaches the floor with 90 J of kinetic energy. So the height stored the work of the lift. This stored energy is called gravitational potential energy, and it belongs to the bag and the Earth together.
A change in potential energy comes from a change in height. Write Δh for the final height minus the initial height. The change in potential energy, ΔU, is then mg × Δh.

afterFigure.text: Raising an object makes Δh positive, so energy is stored. Lowering it makes Δh negative, so the potential energy falls. A 2 kg book moves from a table at 1 m to a shelf at 2.5 m. Then Δh = 1.5 m and ΔU = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J. Lower it back and Δh = −1.5 m, so ΔU = −30 J.

lead.text: A 3 kg object is raised from 1 m to 5 m. Take g as 10 m/s².

reveal.text: You found the height change first, then multiplied by mg: 4 m of rise gave 120 J.

steps.headline: A 4 kg object falls from 9 m to 2 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its potential-energy change.

workedSteps.text: The height change is final minus initial.
The weight is mg.
Multiply the weight by the height change.

steps.headline: What gravity does

lead.text: Return to the lift and look at both forces. You pull up with 60 N and gravity pulls down with 60 N. Over the 1.5 m rise you do +90 J, and gravity does −60 × 1.5 = −90 J, because it points against the move. The two cancel, which is what a steady speed means: the net work is zero, so the kinetic energy does not change.
The potential energy rose by 90 J while gravity did −90 J. That is no coincidence. The work gravity does is always minus the change in potential energy.
Now the other direction. A 1 kg ball drops 3 m, so its potential energy changes by 1 × 10 × (−3) = −30 J. Gravity points along the move and does +30 J of work, so the ball speeds up.
The same 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m. Use the sign of the energy change you found.

reveal.text: A fall lowers potential energy by 100 J, so gravity did +100 J of work.

steps.headline: Where height starts from

lead.text: Heights need a starting point, and the choice is yours. Measured from the floor, a book rises from 1 m to 2.5 m. Measured from a table 0.8 m high, the same rise runs from 0.2 m to 1.7 m. The heights differ, but the height change is 1.5 m both times, so ΔU = mgΔh gives the same 30 J for a 2 kg book either way.

Only differences in height matter, because only changes in potential energy have effects, such as the work gravity does. The choice of zero also says nothing about speed. Kinetic energy depends on how fast an object moves and not on its height, so an object passing the floor can still be moving quickly even when the floor is called zero height.
Two people describe the same rise. One measures height from the floor, the other from the table.

reveal.text: Both readings of height shift together, so the difference, and the energy change, agree.

blocks.text: Lift a box onto a high shelf and you spend effort, and the box ends up higher. Nudge it off the edge later and it drops, speeding up as it goes, just as the bike speeds up on the hill. The fall gives the box motion that nobody paid for at the time.

That motion has to come from somewhere. The last lesson showed that speeding up needs net work, and during the fall only gravity acts on the box. A natural guess is that the effort you spent on the lift was kept somewhere and handed back. If so, the height of the box is where it was kept.

This lesson tests that guess. We count the work in a slow lift, name what the height stores and write a rule for it, then work out what gravity does on the way up and on the way down. The last step asks whether it matters where we call the height zero.

lessons.title: Where the energy goes

steps.headline: A falling ball trades height for speed

lead.text: Take the ball and the Earth together as one system. As the ball falls, its potential energy drops because its height drops, and its kinetic energy rises because it speeds up. The last two lessons gave both changes: gravity's work is minus the change in potential energy, and the net work is the change in kinetic energy. If gravity is the only force doing work, the two are the same work, so the potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained.

Follow a 0.5 kg apple that falls 4 m. At the top its potential energy is 0.5 × 10 × 4 = 20 J and its kinetic energy is 0. Halfway down, at 2 m, the potential energy is 10 J and the kinetic energy is 10 J. At the bottom the potential energy is 0 and the kinetic energy is 20 J.

afterFigure.text: The sum of kinetic and potential energy is called mechanical energy. In the fall it stays at 20 J the whole way, while the split between the two forms keeps changing. The picture shows the same pattern for two other drops.

lead.text: Only gravity does work on the ball, and it lands at height zero.

reveal.text: All 50 J of potential energy became kinetic energy.

steps.headline: When friction takes some of it

lead.text: Now let a crate slide down a rough ramp instead of falling freely. Friction acts on it as it slides, and friction does negative work, so the mechanical energy no longer stays the same. The crate reaches the bottom with less kinetic energy than the potential energy it lost.

The missing energy has not vanished. Rubbing surfaces get warm, and the crate and the ramp both warm up a little. The extra random motion of their atoms is called thermal energy, and it is also measured in joules. Take a 1 kg crate that slides down 3 m, with 10 J of its energy turning into thermal energy. It loses 1 × 10 × 3 = 30 J of potential energy. Of that, 10 J becomes thermal energy and the remaining 20 J is the crate's kinetic energy at the bottom.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the same 1 kg object drops 3 m twice, once with no friction and once on the rough ramp. The extra thermal energy takes its share of the 30 J, and the kinetic energy at the bottom is smaller by that amount.

steps.headline: A 2 kg block slides down from 4 m with g = 10 m/s². 30 J becomes heating. Find its final kinetic energy.

workedSteps.text: Potential energy lost.
Some of it heats the surface.
The rest becomes kinetic energy.

steps.headline: A 2 kg object drops from 10 m with g = 10 m/s². 40 J becomes heating. Find the final kinetic energy.

workedSteps.text: Potential energy lost.
Take off the thermal energy.

steps.headline: From energy to speed

lead.text: An energy account usually ends with a kinetic energy, and often the thing we want is a speed. Start from K = ½mv², multiply both sides by 2 and divide by m. That gives v² = 2K ÷ m, and the speed is the square root of it.

A 2 kg cart with 16 J of kinetic energy has v² = 2 × 16 ÷ 2 = 16, so it moves at 4 m/s. The same steps work on a falling object. From rest at height h with no friction, its kinetic energy at the bottom is mgh, so v² = 2gh. The mass cancels, which agrees with what we saw earlier: heavy and light objects fall at the same rate.
A 2 kg object ends a descent with some kinetic energy. Work out its speed.

reveal.text: With 100 J and 2 kg, v² is 100 and v is 10 m/s.

steps.headline: One account for every case

lead.text: Every example so far fits one statement. The changes in kinetic energy, potential energy and thermal energy add up to zero, as long as nothing outside the system adds energy or takes it away.

Suppose an object starts with 5 J of kinetic energy, drops through a height that costs it 40 J of potential energy, and produces 15 J of thermal energy. Then ΔU = −40 J and ΔE_thermal = +15 J, so ΔK = 40 − 15 = +25 J and the final kinetic energy is 5 + 25 = 30 J.

This is the conservation of energy: the total stays fixed while energy changes form and passes between objects. The crate shows it. Friction lowered its mechanical energy by an amount that appeared as thermal energy.
An object slides down a rough track. The object, Earth and track are one system with nothing else acting on it.

reveal.text: Include the heating and the books balance: kinetic plus potential plus thermal never changes.

A falling ball is the clean case. A crate sliding down a rough ramp is the messy one: it ends up slower than the same drop in free fall would make it, and the crate and the ramp feel warm afterwards. Energy seems to go missing. This lesson keeps an account of the energy through both, and the question is whether the books ever fail to balance.

We follow the falling ball first and see what its energy turns into. Then friction joins the account. After that we find a speed from the energy that is left and write one rule that covers both cases.

recap.keyIdea: Energy is never lost: potential energy becomes kinetic and thermal energy, and the total of every form stays fixed.

lessons.title: Power and efficiency

steps.headline: How fast the energy arrives

lead.text: Start with the kettle. Suppose it takes 2,000 J from the socket every second. After ten seconds it has taken 20,000 J, and after a minute it has taken 120,000 J. A candle gives out perhaps 50 J every second, so it needs forty minutes to supply the same 120,000 J.

The number of joules delivered every second is what sets the two apart, and it has its own name. Power is the energy transferred each second. Its unit is the watt (W), where one watt is one joule per second. By that measure the kettle is rated at 2,000 W. A lamp that transfers 60 J every second is a 60 W lamp.
To find the power of any machine, divide the energy it transfers by the time that takes. A lamp that transfers 600 J in 10 s has a power of 600 ÷ 10 = 60 W. Try the same division on a motor next.
Share the energy the motor uses out over the seconds it takes.

reveal.text: 600 ÷ 3 gives 200 J every second, so the motor's power is 200 W.

steps.headline: The same job, done faster

lead.text: Power ties together three quantities, so it can answer questions beyond the rate itself. Take one job that needs 600 J. A machine that takes 12 s to do it works at 600 ÷ 12 = 50 W. A machine that does the same job in 6 s works at 600 ÷ 6 = 100 W.

Halving the time doubles the power, because the same energy has to move in half as long. Turn the equation round and you get the other two forms: energy = power × time, and time = energy ÷ power. A 2,000 W kettle running for 60 s transfers 2,000 × 60 = 120,000 J, the figure from the last screen.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two cases in the figure. The energy is the same in both and the time differs, which is what makes the power differ. Doing the same job faster needs more power, and that is how the kettle beats the candle. How much of the energy actually does the job is a separate question, and the next few screens come to it after one more problem on the rate.

lead.text: Use the division from the last two screens.

reveal.text: 1,200 ÷ 4 gives 300 J every second, a power of 300 W.

steps.headline: The share that does the job

lead.text: Return to the kettle. It takes 1,000 J from the socket, and the water ends up with 900 J more energy than before. The other 100 J warms the plastic and the air around it. The 900 J is the useful output, the part you wanted, and the 1,000 J is the input.

The useful output as a fraction of the input is 900 ÷ 1,000 = 0.9, or 90%. That fraction is the kettle's efficiency: the useful output energy divided by the input energy, usually quoted as a percentage.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares two kettles that take in the same energy. The second keeps far less of it for the water. No real machine reaches 100%, because every one warms its surroundings a little. A candle under a pan is a poor heater by this measure, since most of its energy warms the room instead of the water. The next screens practise finding an efficiency one line at a time.

steps.headline: A device takes in 2,000 J and delivers 1,200 J of useful output. Find its efficiency.

workedSteps.text: Divide useful output by input.

steps.headline: Where the rest goes

lead.text: Energy cannot disappear, as the last lesson showed, so the 100 J that did not reach the water must be somewhere. It is in the warm plastic and the warm air, and a little of it is the faint sound of the element. Energy that ends up somewhere other than the job is called wasted energy. It still exists, but it has spread out too thinly to collect and use again.

That gives every machine an account that balances. The energy put in equals the useful energy out plus the wasted energy, as long as the machine is not storing any for later. An old filament lamp that takes in 100 J and gives out 5 J as light wastes the other 95 J as heat.

Knowing two of the three amounts always gives you the third. Wasted energy also shows why efficiency and power are different measures. Efficiency says how much of the energy does the job and power says how fast it moves. A machine can do either well and the other badly.
Every joule that goes in has to come out somewhere.

reveal.text: 2,000 − 1,200 leaves 800 J going out as heat, sound or similar.

steps.headline: Rates in and out

lead.text: Efficiency applies to rates as well as totals. A kettle's label gives the rate at which it takes energy from the socket, say 2,000 W. If its efficiency is 90%, then 90% of that rate reaches the water: 1,800 J every second. The other 200 J every second goes to the kettle and the room.

So the useful power out is the efficiency, written as a fraction, multiplied by the power in. The relationship also runs backwards when you know the output and need the input. To deliver 45 W of useful power at 90% efficiency, a machine needs 45 ÷ 0.9 = 50 W going in. You divide by the efficiency because the input is always the larger number.
A machine is rebuilt to do the same job as before in half the time.

reveal.text: Power doubles because the same energy takes half as long.

Both are heating the water, and the water needs the same amount of energy to reach the same temperature either way, so the difference has to be in how fast the energy arrives.

The kettle delivers its energy quickly and the candle delivers it slowly. If you knew how many joules each one gave out every second, you could compare them straight away and work out how long any heating job would take. There is a second thing worth knowing about the kettle. Some of the energy it takes from the socket warms the kettle itself and the air around it, and only the rest reaches the water.
This lesson follows the energy through a kettle. We start with how fast it arrives. After that we measure how much of it does the job and where the remainder goes.

lessons.title: Momentum and impulse

steps.headline: What a moving thing carries

lead.text: Think about stopping two things that move at the same speed, a tennis ball and a bowling ball, both rolling towards you at walking pace. The tennis ball is easy to stop and the bowling ball is hard. Take one bowling ball and roll it faster and it becomes harder again. How hard something is to stop depends on its mass and on its velocity.

Physicists multiply the two together and call the result momentum. Momentum = mass × velocity, written p = mv, and its unit is the kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s). A 1 kg ball moving at 5 m/s has a momentum of 5 kg·m/s. A 10 kg bowling ball at the same velocity has 50 kg·m/s.

Velocity has a direction, so momentum has a direction too. It takes its sign from the velocity. With right taken as positive, a 1 kg ball moving left at 7 m/s has a momentum of −7 kg·m/s. Kinetic energy has no direction, because it depends on the speed squared.
Take right as positive and use the sign of the velocity.

reveal.text: You multiplied the mass by the signed velocity, and rightward motion gives a positive result.

steps.headline: A push that lasts for a time

lead.text: Momentum changes when something pushes. Push a stationary trolley with a steady force and it starts to move. Keep pushing and it moves faster. Two things decide how much momentum you give it: how hard you push and how long you keep pushing. A strong push that lasts a split second can give the same as a gentle push that lasts a long time.

The force multiplied by the time it acts for is called impulse. Impulse = F × Δt, where Δt means the time the force acts for. Its unit is the newton second (N·s) and it takes its sign from the force. An impulse equals the change in momentum that it produces. That change is written Δp and is the final momentum minus the initial momentum.

afterFigure.text: Suppose a steady 10 N push acts on a 5 kg trolley for 3 s. The impulse is 10 × 3 = 30 N·s, so a trolley that started at rest ends with 30 kg·m/s. The figure shows that push lasting 3 s and then 1 s. The longer push gives three times the impulse, so it leaves the trolley with three times the momentum. In every case the force here is the net force, the total of everything pushing on the trolley.

lead.text: Use the size of the force and how long it lasts.

reveal.text: 6 × 3 gives an impulse of +18 N·s.

steps.headline: From a push to a final velocity

lead.text: Because impulse equals the change in momentum, final momentum = initial momentum + impulse. Take a 4 kg cart rolling right at 1 m/s. Its momentum is 4 × 1 = 4 kg·m/s. A net impulse of +12 N·s takes that to 16 kg·m/s. Momentum is mass times velocity, so divide by the mass: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 m/s.

The sign of the impulse matters, because an impulse that points against the motion takes momentum away. An impulse of −4 N·s brings the same cart's momentum to zero and stops it. A larger impulse of −12 N·s turns it round, since 4 − 12 = −8 kg·m/s, which is 2 m/s to the left.
To find a final velocity, start from the initial momentum and add the impulse with its sign. Then divide by the mass. The next screen works through this on a pushed cart.

steps.headline: Why a longer stop is gentler

lead.text: Back to the ball. Catching it brings its momentum to zero, so the impulse needed depends only on how much momentum it has. A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s carries 10 kg·m/s, so catching it takes an impulse of −10 N·s whatever your hands do.

Impulse is force times time, so the force is the impulse divided by the time: F = Δp ÷ Δt. This is the average net force during the stop. Stop the ball in 0.5 s and the average force is −10 ÷ 0.5 = −20 N. Stop it in 2 s and the average force is −10 ÷ 2 = −5 N. The minus sign says the force points against the motion.

afterFigure.text: Both cases in the figure remove the same momentum, but the longer stop needs a quarter of the force. Hands drawn back, a crash helmet and a car's crumple zone all work this way. They cannot change the momentum that has to go, so they spread its removal over more time.

lead.text: The ball has to lose the same momentum whichever way it is caught. Only the time changes.

reveal.text: The same impulse of 20 N·s spread over 2 s needs 10 N.

lead.text: Stopping takes the cart's momentum down to zero over the time given.

reveal.text: The cart loses 24 kg·m/s over 3 s, an average force of −8 N.

steps.headline: When the motion reverses

lead.text: A ball that hits a wall and comes back changes more than it seems to. Take a 3 kg trolley moving right at 5 m/s that bounces off a spring and returns at 5 m/s to the left. Its speed is the same, so its kinetic energy is the same before and after: ½ × 3 × 5² = 37.5 J.

Its momentum is different. Before the bounce it is 3 × 5 = +15 kg·m/s. After it is 3 × (−5) = −15 kg·m/s. The change is −15 − 15 = −30 kg·m/s, so the spring gave the trolley an impulse of −30 N·s. That is twice the momentum the trolley started with, because the spring first had to remove the rightward momentum and then build the same amount in the other direction.
This is the difference between the two quantities. Kinetic energy follows only the speed, and momentum follows the velocity with its sign.
A 2 kg cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s.

reveal.text: Speed squared is the same, so kinetic energy is the same. Momentum changes by −16 kg·m/s.

The ball arrives at the same speed both times and has to be brought to a stop both times, so the difference must lie in how the stop happens.

What differs is the time. Stiff hands stop the ball in a flash and hands that give way take longer. The sting is a force, and the force needed to stop a ball depends on how long you take over it. To put numbers on that, we need a way to say how much motion the ball carries and a way to say how a push changes it.

lessons.title: When carts stick together

steps.headline: What a crash does to momentum

lead.text: Start at the moment of the crash. When the front of one cart meets the back of the other, each pushes on the other. You met this in the lesson on pairs of forces: the two pushes are equal in size and opposite in direction, and they last exactly as long as the carts stay in contact.

Equal and opposite forces acting for the same time give equal and opposite impulses. One cart gains as much momentum as the other loses. If you add the two momenta together, the gain and the loss cancel, so the total is the same after the crash as before. This is called conservation of momentum.
For now we assume that the carts are pushed only by each other during the crash. The last screens come back to what happens when something else pushes too.

steps.headline: One total, shared by the stuck pair

lead.text: Now let the carts stick. After the crash they move as a single object with one velocity, and its mass is the two masses added together. Its momentum is that mass times the shared velocity, and by conservation this equals the total momentum before the crash.

Here u means a velocity before the crash and v is the shared velocity after it. Take a 1 kg cart moving at 5 m/s that locks onto a 4 kg cart standing still. The momentum before is 1 × 5 + 4 × 0 = 5 kg·m/s, because a cart at rest has none. Afterwards the 5 kg pair carries the same 5 kg·m/s, so its velocity is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 m/s.

afterFigure.text: The moving cart handed over some of its momentum, and the larger mass left it moving more slowly. The figure shows this crash, and a second one where the front cart is already rolling. Look at how the shared velocity changes with the starting velocity of the front cart.

lead.text: Both carts have the same mass, and the moving one is the only one with momentum.

reveal.text: The pair has twice the mass and the same momentum, so its speed is halved.

lead.text: Find the total momentum before the crash, then divide by the mass of the pair.

reveal.text: The momentum is 12 kg·m/s, shared by 6 kg, giving 2 m/s.

steps.headline: Carts that approach from opposite ends

lead.text: So far both carts moved the same way. Carts can also approach each other from opposite ends of the track, and then the signs matter. Take right as positive. A cart moving right has positive momentum and a cart moving left has negative momentum, so adding them lets one cancel part of the other.

Try a 2 kg cart moving right at 5 m/s and a 3 kg cart moving left at 2 m/s. Their momenta are 2 × 5 = +10 kg·m/s and 3 × (−2) = −6 kg·m/s. The total is +4 kg·m/s. The pair weighs 5 kg, so it moves at 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 m/s to the right.

The sign of the total tells you which way the pair ends up, and a total of zero would leave it at rest. Always give each momentum its sign before you add, and divide by the combined mass only at the end.

steps.headline: What happens to the kinetic energy

lead.text: Momentum survives the crash and kinetic energy does not. Go back to the 1 kg cart at 5 m/s that locked onto the 4 kg cart. Before the crash its kinetic energy was ½ × 1 × 5² = 12.5 J. Afterwards the 5 kg pair moves at 1 m/s and has ½ × 5 × 1² = 2.5 J. The crash used up 10 J, four fifths of what there was.

The missing energy went into other forms. The couplings banged together and the metal deformed a little. The crash made a noise and warmed the carts. This is the energy account from the earlier lessons again: kinetic energy became thermal energy and sound. A collision that turns kinetic energy into other forms like this is called an inelastic collision, and carts that stick together lose the most they can.
The two rules do different jobs. Momentum gives you the speed of the pair, and the energy account tells you what the crash cost.
Work out the kinetic energy before the crash and after it, and compare.

reveal.text: The kinetic energy drops from 36 J to 12 J, so 24 J became other forms.

steps.headline: When the rule holds

lead.text: The rule needs a condition. Total momentum stays the same only if no outside impulse acts on the two carts. The pushes the carts give each other are internal forces, and because they come in equal and opposite pairs they cancel in the total whatever their size. A push from outside brings an impulse that nothing cancels. A hand holding the first cart back would do it, and so would a rough floor dragging on the wheels.

On a smooth track a crash lasts so short a time that the impulse from friction is tiny beside the carts' momentum, and ignoring it is reasonable. The same reasoning applies to any crash between two objects, whether or not they stick. On any new problem, check first whether anything outside is pushing on the objects during the crash.
The carts push each other during the crash. The track and the air might push them as well.

reveal.text: Internal forces cancel in the total, so only a significant outside impulse could change it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two readings. Displacement is a difference: final minus initial.

questions.prompt: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
hints: Count both stretches of the trip.
Each stretch has length 7 − 1 metres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.

questions.onCorrect: 12 m. Distance adds every stretch of the path, so the trip back counts as well as the trip out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the cart ended from where it began. Distance counts every stretch it travelled.
That is the trip out only. The cart also has to come back.

questions.prompt: The origin shifts so that a trip from 2 m to 9 m is recorded as 12 m to 19 m. What happens to the displacement?
hints: Compare the differences between the two pairs of endpoints.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both readings increase by 10 m; their difference stays +7 m.

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Both readings rise by the same amount, so their difference does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the readings change, not the trip. Both ends move by the same amount, so the gap between them does not grow.
Nothing in the trip doubled. Compare the gap between the two readings in each pair.

questions.prompt: A robot moves from 0 m to 8 m, then back to 3 m. How far does it travel altogether, in metres?
hints: Break the trip at the turning point.
The return stretch runs from 8 m to 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.

questions.onCorrect: 13 m. Break the trip at the turning point and add the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the robot ended from where it began. The distance counts the whole path.
That is the trip out only. The robot also travels back.
That is the return stretch only. Count the trip out as well.

questions.prompt: A lift's marked position changes from 5 m to −4 m. With upward positive, find its displacement in metres.
hints: Keep the minus sign on the final position.
Subtract the initial position from the final position.
Calculate −4 − 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.

questions.onCorrect: −9 m. Final minus initial gives a negative number when the move is in the negative direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the lift went down. With upward positive, a downward move needs a minus sign.
That adds the two readings. Take the start away from the finish.

questions.prompt: A cart travels from −2 m to 4 m and then to 1 m. Which statement describes its trip?
hints: Use endpoints for displacement and both path lengths for distance.

acceptedIdeas: Displacement 3 m; distance 9 m
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: Displacement compares the ends: 3 m. Distance adds both stretches: 9 m.

misconceptions.feedback: These are swapped. The ends give the displacement, and the whole path gives the distance.
The cart finishes at a larger position than it started, so its displacement is not negative.

questions.prompt: A rover covers 18 m in 6 s without reversing. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Use total distance and elapsed time.
Divide distance by time.
Share the travelled distance equally across the elapsed seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the distance by the time. Speed is distance shared out over time, so divide.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per unit of time.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. Find its average velocity in m/s.
hints: Velocity keeps the direction of displacement.
Divide the signed displacement by elapsed time.
Divide the displacement magnitude by duration and keep its negative sign.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m/s. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement, so a leftward move gives a negative velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart moved left. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: A runner goes 10 m from a marker and returns to that marker in a total of 5 s. Find the average velocity in m/s.
hints: Use the final and initial positions.
A return to the same point leaves no displacement.
Divide that displacement by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s. The runner ends where they began, so the displacement is zero whatever the distance run.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed for the out leg only. Velocity uses the displacement over the whole trip.
That divides the distance there and back by the time. Velocity uses displacement, not distance.

questions.prompt: A robot travels 6 m in 2 s, then 6 m in 4 s. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
hints: Combine distances and times before dividing.

acceptedIdeas: 2 m/s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s, giving 2 m/s. The slower section lasts longer.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. Add the distances, add the times, then divide. Averaging the two speeds would over-weight the fast stretch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean of the two stretch speeds. The slower stretch lasts longer, so it should count for more.
That is the speed of the first stretch only. Use the whole trip.

questions.prompt: A conveyor moves a parcel 42 m along a straight path in 7 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Identify the path length and duration.
Use distance divided by time.
Find how many metres correspond to one second.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Distance divided by time, with the path length and the duration both read from the problem.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Divide the distance by the time.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per second.

questions.prompt: A moving object returns to its start. Which average must be zero over the complete trip?
hints: Ask which average uses displacement.

acceptedIdeas: Average velocity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.

questions.onCorrect: Average velocity. A return to the start makes the displacement zero; the distance travelled stays positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Average speed uses distance, and the distance run is not zero. Which average uses displacement?
Only one of them uses displacement. The other uses the distance, which cannot be zero for a trip.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time segment goes from 2 m at 0 s to 14 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Read the changes on both axes.
Divide position change by time change.
Calculate (14 − 2)/3.
questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Rise over run on a position–time graph is velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the time the change took.
That divides time by position. The slope is position change per unit time.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph is horizontal from 2 s to 4 s. What does the object do during that interval?
hints: Compare the position at the ends of the horizontal segment.

acceptedIdeas: Stays at the same position
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position stays fixed during the interval, so the object is stationary.

choices.label: Moves at a positive constant speed

questions.onCorrect: Flat means the position does not change, so the object is at rest during that time.

misconceptions.feedback: Constant speed would need a line that rises or falls. This line stays at one height.
Accelerating would show a curve. A level line means no change in position at all.

questions.prompt: Position falls from 10 m to 2 m along a straight graph segment lasting 4 s. Find the velocity in m/s.
hints: A falling position reading has a negative change.
Use final position minus initial position.
Calculate (2 − 10)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. A falling position line means a negative velocity. Final minus initial, over the time.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position is falling. The velocity has to be negative.
That is the change in position alone. Divide by the time it took.

questions.prompt: A graph starts at 0 m at 0 s and finishes at 2 m at 6 s, with a pause and reversal between. Find the overall average velocity in m/s; a fraction is accepted.
hints: Use the outer endpoints for the full interval.
Include the entire elapsed time, including the pause.
Divide 2 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 1/3 m/s. Use the outer endpoints and the whole time. The pause and the turn still count as time.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the position change by the wrong time. Use the full 6 seconds.
That drops the pause from the time. The time on the graph runs from start to finish.

questions.prompt: A straight graph segment runs from x = 3 m at t = 1 s to x = 15 m at t = 4 s. Find its velocity in m/s.
hints: Subtract the earlier reading from the later reading on each axis.
Subtract the earlier time from the later time.
Divide the change in position by the change in time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Subtract on both axes, then divide: the change in position over the change in time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position. Divide by the change in time as well.
That divides the later position by the later time. Use the changes, not the readings.

questions.prompt: What does a straight rising line on a position–time graph indicate?
hints: A graph of position against time shows a rate, not the shape of the road.

acceptedIdeas: Constant positive velocity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.

questions.onCorrect: A straight rising line means equal position steps in equal times: constant positive velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph plots position against time. It does not show the slope of a road.
Increasing velocity would bend the line upward. A straight line has one constant slope.

questions.prompt: A cart changes velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Find the signed change in velocity.
Divide that change by the elapsed time.
Subtract initial from final velocity, then divide by duration.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s². Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in velocity. Divide by the time to get a rate.
That divides the final velocity by the time. Use the change in velocity.

questions.prompt: Velocity changes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Subtract the initial negative velocity carefully.
The velocity moves toward zero.
Calculate (−2 − (−8))/3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The velocity change is −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s. Dividing by 3 s gives +2 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Velocity rose from −8 to −2, so acceleration is positive even though the cart is slowing.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart is slowing, but acceleration is final minus initial velocity. That change is positive.
That adds the two velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A cart has negative velocity and negative acceleration. What happens to its speed while those signs remain?
hints: Compare the directions, rather than interpreting a minus sign as braking.

acceptedIdeas: Its speed increases
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Velocity and acceleration both point left, so the magnitude of velocity increases.

questions.onCorrect: Its speed increases. Velocity and acceleration point the same way, so the cart speeds up.

misconceptions.feedback: A minus sign alone does not mean slowing down. Compare the directions of velocity and acceleration.
Nothing here makes the velocity zero. It only grows in the direction it already points.

questions.prompt: A cart keeps a velocity of 6 m/s for 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Acceleration depends on a change in velocity.
Compare the initial and final velocities.
Calculate (6 − 6)/4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is no velocity change: (6 − 6)/4 = 0 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s². Velocity did not change, so there is no acceleration, though the cart keeps moving.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the velocity. Acceleration is how much the velocity changes.
That divides the velocity by the time. Acceleration needs a change in velocity.

questions.prompt: A robot's velocity changes from 9 m/s to −3 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: The final velocity points opposite to the initial velocity.
Keep signs when subtracting.
Divide the negative velocity change by elapsed time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is −3 − 9 = −12 m/s. Acceleration is −12/4 = −3 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −3 m/s². The velocity change is final minus initial, and it is negative because the robot reverses.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the velocity falls. The sign has to show that.
That adds the velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A cart's velocity changes steadily from positive to negative, passing through zero on the way. At the instant its velocity is zero, which description is possible?
hints: Think of a cart that rolls up a slope and stops for an instant before it rolls back.

acceptedIdeas: Zero velocity with nonzero acceleration
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The graph's value is zero at the crossing, while its slope remains nonzero.

choices.label: Zero velocity must mean zero acceleration

questions.onCorrect: Zero velocity with nonzero acceleration. A velocity can pass through zero while it is still changing.

misconceptions.feedback: Velocity and acceleration are separate quantities. A cart can pass through zero velocity while its velocity is still changing.
The velocity changes steadily, so the acceleration has one value throughout. It does not switch off at zero.

questions.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m/s and has constant acceleration 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the velocity added during the interval.
Multiply acceleration by time, then add the initial velocity.
Calculate 3 + 2 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 11 m/s. Constant acceleration adds the same velocity every second: start plus acceleration times time.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds one second's gain only. The cart gains it every second for 4 s.
That is the velocity gained. The cart also started with some velocity.

questions.prompt: Starting at 3 m/s, a cart accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: You already have the average velocity from the lines above.
Distance covered is average velocity times time.
Multiply the 7 m/s by the 4 s.
questions.onCorrect: 28 m. Average velocity times time, with the average taken halfway between start and finish.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance if the cart held its starting velocity. It speeds up, so it covers more.
That uses at² without the half. Average the start and finish velocities instead.

questions.prompt: An object starts from rest with constant nonzero acceleration. Doubling the travel time multiplies its displacement by what factor?
hints: Track the exponent on time in ½at².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement is proportional to time squared; doubling time gives a factor of 2² = 4.

questions.onCorrect: A factor of 4. From rest, displacement grows with time squared, so doubling the time quadruples it.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the time also doubles the final velocity, so the distance grows by more than a factor of two.
That would need time cubed. Displacement from rest goes as time squared.

questions.prompt: A cart brakes uniformly from 12 m/s to rest in 4 s. Find its stopping distance in metres.
hints: Uniform braking makes the velocity change linearly.
Average the initial and final velocities.
Multiply (12 + 0)/2 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average velocity is (12 + 0)/2 = 6 m/s. Displacement is 6 × 4 = 24 m.

questions.onCorrect: 24 m. Uniform braking makes the average velocity the mean of start and finish; multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the cart as moving at its starting velocity throughout. It slows down, so it goes less far.
That is the average velocity. Multiply it by the time to get a distance.

questions.prompt: A robot begins at x = 5 m with velocity 2 m/s and constant acceleration 1 m/s². Find its position after 4 s, in metres.
hints: First find displacement, then add the initial position.
Use x = x₀ + ut + ½at².
Calculate 5 + 8 + 8.
questions.onCorrect: 21 m. Start position, plus distance from the initial velocity, plus the extra from accelerating.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the extra distance gained by accelerating. Add ½at² as well.
That leaves out the half in ½at². Check the last term.

questions.prompt: When is displacement = ut + ½at² valid for the whole interval?
hints: Identify the assumption used to combine the velocity changes.

acceptedIdeas: When acceleration is constant over the interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This expression assumes constant acceleration during the interval; direction alone is not enough.

choices.label: When acceleration is constant over the interval

questions.onCorrect: Only when acceleration is constant over the interval. That is the assumption the formula is built on.

misconceptions.feedback: Starting from rest is a special case of the formula, not a condition for using it.
The direction of motion does not matter. What matters is that the acceleration stays the same.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from rest. Take upward as positive and g = 10 m/s², with no air resistance. Find its velocity after 2 s, in m/s.
hints: Gravity points opposite to the positive direction.
Use negative acceleration in v = u + at.
Calculate 0 − 10 × 2.
questions.onCorrect: −20 m/s. The ball gains 10 m/s of downward velocity each second, and downward is negative here.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the ball moves down. With upward positive, its velocity is negative.
That is the velocity after one second only. The ball keeps gaining speed for 2 s.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from height 45 m. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, what is its height after 2 s, in metres?
hints: Find the downward displacement from rest.
Subtract ½gt² from the starting height.
Calculate 45 − 0.5 × 10 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 25 m. Height is the start plus the signed displacement, and falling gives a negative displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the fall to the starting height. The ball goes down, so subtract it.
That uses the distance for 1 s of falling. The ball falls for 2 s.

questions.prompt: At the highest point of a vertical throw, find the acceleration in m/s². Take upward positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance.
hints: Separate zero velocity from zero acceleration.
Gravity continues acting throughout the flight.
Use the downward value of g with upward positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.

questions.onCorrect: −10 m/s². Velocity is zero at the top for an instant, but gravity keeps pulling down.

misconceptions.feedback: The velocity is zero there, not the acceleration. Gravity still acts at the top.
The size is right, but the pull is downward. With upward positive it needs a minus sign.

questions.prompt: Two objects of different mass are released together from the same height in the same gravitational field. Ignore air resistance. Which lands first?
hints: Check whether mass appears in the free-fall position equation.

acceptedIdeas: They land together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.

questions.onCorrect: They land together. Without air resistance, free-fall acceleration does not depend on mass.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger weight is balanced by a bigger mass to move. Without air resistance, the two cancel.
Mass does not appear in the free-fall equations. Both objects move the same way.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 30 m/s. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, find its displacement after 2 s in metres.
hints: Combine the initial upward motion with the downward acceleration.
Use ut − ½gt².
Calculate 60 − 20.
questions.onCorrect: 40 m. Distance from the initial velocity, minus the amount gravity takes back.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores gravity. The ball slows as it rises, so it goes less far than that.
That subtracts the wrong way round. Gravity takes distance off, it does not add.

questions.prompt: While a freely thrown ball is moving upward, which direction does its acceleration point? Ignore air resistance.
hints: The direction of motion does not determine the direction of gravitational acceleration.

acceptedIdeas: Downward, toward Earth
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.

choices.label: Upward, because the ball is rising
It has no acceleration until it falls

questions.onCorrect: Downward, towards Earth. Gravity gives the same downward acceleration on the way up, at the top and on the way down.

misconceptions.feedback: The direction of motion does not set the direction of acceleration. A rising ball is slowing.
Gravity acts the moment the ball leaves the hand, not when it starts to fall.

questions.prompt: Two horizontal forces act on a cart: 14 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Give opposite directions opposite signs.
Add the signed forces on the same cart.
Calculate 14 − 6.
questions.onCorrect: +8 N. Net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object, with opposite directions given opposite signs.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. The leftward force pulls against the rightward one, so subtract.
The size is right, but the larger force points right. The net force is positive.

questions.prompt: A cart is rolling right at 3 m/s on a track with no friction, and the net force on it stays zero. What happens next?
hints: Balanced forces imply no change in velocity.

acceptedIdeas: It continues at 3 m/s to the right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero net force leaves the velocity unchanged.

choices.label: It continues at 3 m/s to the right

questions.onCorrect: It keeps going at 3 m/s to the right. Zero net force means no change in velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: Stopping would need a net force opposing the motion. Balanced forces leave the velocity as it is.
Gaining speed would need a net force in the direction of motion. Here it is zero.

questions.prompt: A resting cart has 9 N rightward and 9 N leftward horizontal forces. Find its horizontal net force in newtons.
hints: Compare the two force magnitudes.
Use opposite signs for opposite directions.
Calculate 9 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 0 N. Equal forces in opposite directions add to zero: balanced forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. The forces point opposite ways, so one takes the other away.
That is one of the two forces. Add both with their signs.

questions.prompt: A cart moving right experiences 8 N right and 20 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Separate the velocity direction from the force sum.
The leftward force enters with a minus sign.
Calculate 8 − 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 20 = −12 N. The net force is leftward even while the cart moves right.

questions.onCorrect: −12 N. The net force points left even though the cart moves right: it slows the cart down.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The net force is negative.
That adds the sizes. The two forces point opposite ways, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Forces of 7 N and 11 N act rightward on a crate; a 5 N force acts leftward. Find the net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Group the forces pointing in the same direction.
Add the two rightward forces, then subtract the leftward force.
Calculate 7 + 11 − 5.
questions.onCorrect: +13 N. Add the rightward forces, then take off the leftward one.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the rightward forces are larger. The net force is positive.
That adds all three as if they pointed the same way. The 5 N force points the other way.

questions.prompt: An object moves left at a constant velocity that is not zero. What is the net force on it?
hints: A continuing velocity does not require a continuing net push.

acceptedIdeas: Zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the forces on the object balance.

misconceptions.feedback: A net leftward force would make it accelerate leftward. Its velocity is not changing.
A net rightward force would slow it down. Its velocity is not changing.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart has horizontal forces of 18 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: Add the forces before applying the second law.
Divide the net force by mass.
Calculate (18 − 6)/3.
questions.onCorrect: 4 m/s². Add the forces to get the net force, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the net force. Divide it by the mass to get the acceleration.
That divides one force by the mass. Use the net force of both.

questions.prompt: The mass doubles while the net force stays the same. What happens to acceleration?
hints: Keep the numerator fixed in a = F_net/m.

acceptedIdeas: It is halved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

questions.onCorrect: It is halved. The same net force spread over twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger mass is harder to accelerate, not easier. Mass is on the bottom of a = F ÷ m.
Mass is in the formula, so changing it changes the acceleration.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart experiences a net force of 24 N rightward. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: The stated force is already the net force.
Use acceleration = net force divided by mass.
Divide the stated net force by the cart's mass.
questions.onCorrect: 12 m/s². The force given is already the net force, so divide it by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. To find acceleration, divide the force by the mass.
That subtracts the mass. Divide the force by it.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving right has forces of 4 N right and 12 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: The velocity does not change the force sum.
Subtract the leftward force and divide by mass.
Calculate (4 − 12)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s². The net force is leftward, so the acceleration is leftward whatever way the cart is moving.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The acceleration is negative.
That drops the 4 N rightward force. Both forces count towards the net force.

questions.prompt: What net force, in newtons, gives a 4 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?
hints: This time, the mass and acceleration are known.
Multiply them to find net force.
Calculate 4 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Net force is mass times acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides acceleration by mass. To find a force, multiply them.
That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A heavier cart and a lighter cart must have the same acceleration. Which needs the larger net force?
hints: Hold acceleration fixed in the second law.

acceptedIdeas: The heavier cart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.

choices.label: Both need the same net force

questions.onCorrect: The heavier cart. For the same acceleration, F = ma grows with the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The lighter cart needs less force for the same acceleration, because it has less mass to move.
Mass sets how much force a given acceleration needs, so the two carts differ.

questions.prompt: An object has mass 3 kg where g = 10 m/s². Find the magnitude of its weight in newtons.
hints: Weight is a force produced by gravity.
Multiply mass by the stated gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 3 × 10.
questions.onCorrect: 30 N. Weight is mass times g: the gravitational force on the object.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object moves to a location with smaller gravitational acceleration. What happens to its mass?
hints: Mass and weight measure different physical quantities.

acceptedIdeas: It stays 3 kg
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the gravitational field changes weight; the object's mass remains 3 kg.

questions.onCorrect: It stays 3 kg. Mass belongs to the object; only the weight changes with the field.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is the amount of matter, which does not change with place. Weight is what changes.
Weight is a force in newtons and mass is in kilograms. They are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only its weight and the upward support force act, with g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: At rest, the vertical net force is zero.
The two vertical forces must have equal magnitudes.
Calculate the weight 4 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no vertical acceleration, the support force balances the weight: mg = 4 × 10 = 40 N.

questions.onCorrect: 40 N. At rest the net force is zero, so the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. The support force must match the weight, which is mg.
Gravity is pulling down, so something must be pushing up to keep the object at rest.

questions.prompt: A support accelerates a 4 kg object upward at 2 m/s². Only support and weight act, and g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: The support has to balance the weight and also give a net upward force.
Use support force = m(g + a).
Add g and the acceleration, then multiply by the mass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Support force − mg = ma, so the support force = 4 × (10 + 2) = 48 N.

questions.onCorrect: 48 N. The support carries the weight and supplies extra force to accelerate the object upward.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The object is also accelerating upward, which needs more.
That is the extra force for the acceleration alone. The support also carries the weight.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg object is in a field where g = 9.8 m/s². Find its weight magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the given value of g rather than rounding it to 10.
Multiply mass by gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 7 × 9.8.
questions.onCorrect: 68.6 N. Use the g you are given: weight is mass times g.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds g to 10. The question gives 9.8, so use it.
That divides the mass by g. Weight is mass times g.

questions.prompt: An object on a support moves downward at a constant velocity. Only its weight and the support force act. How does the support force compare with the weight?
hints: Downward velocity does not imply downward acceleration.

acceptedIdeas: It is equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity gives zero acceleration, so the support and weight balance.

questions.onCorrect: Equal. Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the support balances the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller support force would leave a net downward force and the object would speed up downward.
A larger support force would give a net upward force and the object would slow down.

questions.prompt: B pushes A left with a force of 10 N. Find the magnitude of A's force on B in newtons.
hints: Identify the two objects in the interaction.
The two forces have equal magnitudes.
The partner force has the same magnitude and opposite direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Newton's third law gives an equal magnitude: 10 N, directed right.

questions.onCorrect: 10 N. The partner force is equal in size and opposite in direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The forces do not cancel here: they act on different objects. Each is the same size.
The two forces have the same size. They are not added together.

questions.prompt: Cart A pushes a 5 kg cart B right with 10 N. This is B's only horizontal force. Find B's acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Apply the second law to B alone.
Divide the force on B by B's mass.
Divide the interaction force by B's mass.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Apply the second law to B alone: the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
B is pushed right, so its acceleration is positive.

questions.prompt: Cart A has mass 2 kg. Its only horizontal force is 10 N left. With right positive, find A's acceleration in m/s².
hints: Use the mass of the object being accelerated.
The leftward force has a negative sign.
Divide the leftward force magnitude by mass and retain its sign.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s². The force on A is leftward, so its acceleration is negative. Divide by A's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but A is pushed left. With right positive, its acceleration is negative.
That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by A's mass.

questions.prompt: Two carts, A and B, push each other and nothing else pushes on them horizontally. Why do their two forces cancel when we add up the forces on the pair of carts taken together?
hints: Choose a boundary containing both interacting objects.

acceptedIdeas: They are equal, opposite internal forces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For the combined system, the pair is internal and sums to zero. Each cart can still accelerate.

choices.label: They act on the same cart
They are equal, opposite internal forces

questions.onCorrect: They are equal, opposite internal forces. Inside the combined system they sum to zero, yet each cart still accelerates.

misconceptions.feedback: The two forces act on different carts, one on each. That is why each cart accelerates.
Each cart has an unbalanced force on it, so both accelerate. The cancelling is only for the pair taken together.

questions.prompt: Two carts interact with forces of magnitude 18 N. Cart B has mass 6 kg and no other horizontal force. Find its acceleration magnitude in m/s².
hints: Use the force acting on B.
Equal interaction forces do not require equal accelerations.
Divide the force magnitude by the mass of B.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². B's acceleration is the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
The forces on the two carts do not cancel. Each acts on a different cart.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which force is the partner of the table's upward force on the book?
hints: A third-law pair acts on different objects.

acceptedIdeas: The book's downward force on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The paired force swaps the two objects: book on table, opposite to table on book.

choices.label: Earth's downward gravitational force on the book
The book's downward force on the table

questions.onCorrect: The book's downward force on the table. A pair swaps the objects: table on book, book on table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different force on the same book. A pair always acts on two different objects, one force on each.
Mass is not a force. The partner of a force is another force.

questions.prompt: A resting 4 kg box has g = 10 m/s² and static coefficient 0.5. A 12 N horizontal push does not move it. Find the static-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: Is the box accelerating?
What must the total horizontal force on it be?
Which force cancels the push, and is the push above or below the 20 N ceiling?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 12 N push is below the 20 N limit, so static friction is 12 N.

questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Static friction adjusts to match the push, as long as the push stays under the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit, the most static friction can give. Here it only has to match the push.
The box does not move, so something is holding it back. That is friction.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box rests on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces. Use g = 10 m/s² and μ_s = 0.5. Find maximum static friction in newtons.
hints: First find the support force.
Multiply mg by the static coefficient.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 10.
questions.onCorrect: 20 N. The support force is mg, and the limit is the static coefficient times that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the support force. Multiply it by the coefficient as well.
That is the coefficient times the mass. Include g: the support force is mg.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides on a horizontal surface. With g = 10 m/s², no vertical acceleration and μ_k = 0.3, find the sliding-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the coefficient for sliding.
The support force equals mg.
Calculate 0.3 × 40.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Sliding friction is the sliding coefficient times the support force.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the static coefficient. A sliding box uses the sliding coefficient.
That multiplies by the mass without g. The support force is mg.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides right. A 24 N push acts right and sliding friction is 12 N left. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Combine the opposing horizontal forces.
Divide net force by mass.
Calculate (24 − 12)/4.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². Subtract the friction from the push to get the net force, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the push alone by the mass. Friction takes some of it away.
That divides the push alone by the mass. Take friction off first.

questions.prompt: A box can hold at most 30 N of static friction. You push it horizontally with 8 N and it stays at rest. How big is the friction force on it?
hints: Use zero acceleration while the box remains at rest.

acceptedIdeas: 8 N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Static friction balances the 8 N push; 30 N is a limit, not its automatic value.

questions.onCorrect: 8 N. At rest, friction exactly matches the push; the limit is only the most it could give.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit is the most friction can give. It does not set the friction until the push reaches it.
The two do not add. Friction opposes the push, and at rest they balance.

questions.prompt: A sliding box slows to rest on a horizontal floor after its push is removed. What happens to the friction once the box has stopped?
hints: Friction opposes sliding or a tendency to slide; it is not a constant backward motor.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once sliding stops and no horizontal force tries to move it, friction is zero.

choices.label: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
It keeps sliding at a smaller constant speed

questions.onCorrect: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction. Friction opposes sliding; it does not push backward on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: Friction only opposes sliding. Once the box stops, nothing is trying to move it.
A box that has stopped stays stopped. Friction never starts it moving again.

questions.prompt: A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement. Find its work in joules.
hints: Force and displacement point the same way.
Multiply their magnitudes.
Calculate 15 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 60 J. A force along the displacement does positive work: force times distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A constant 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its signed work in joules.
hints: An opposing force does negative work.
Multiply force and distance, retaining the negative sign.
Calculate −6 × 5.
questions.onCorrect: −30 J. A force against the displacement does negative work: it takes energy away.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force opposes the motion. Its work is negative.
That subtracts the numbers. Work is force times distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 20 N upward support force acts during a 3 m horizontal displacement. Find the work done by this support force in joules.
hints: Look for the force component along displacement.
The vertical force has no horizontal component.
A zero component gives zero work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The force is perpendicular to displacement, so its work is 0 J.

questions.onCorrect: 0 J. A force at right angles to the displacement does no work.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance. The force is at right angles to the motion, so none of it acts along it.
That is the distance. Work needs a part of the force along it, and there is none.

questions.prompt: A constant 10 N pull acts along a 7 m displacement. Find the work done by this pull alone in joules.
hints: The question asks about one force, not the net force.
Use W = Fd for this parallel pull.
Calculate 10 × 7.
questions.onCorrect: 70 J. The pull's work depends on that pull alone, not on other forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides the force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: You hold a box stationary for 5 s. How much work does your support force do on the box during that time?
hints: Mechanical work depends on displacement, not the duration of effort.

acceptedIdeas: Zero work because displacement is zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The box has no displacement, so this support force does zero mechanical work on it.

choices.label: Zero work because displacement is zero

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Work needs displacement: a force that moves nothing does no mechanical work.

misconceptions.feedback: Time passing does not count. Work needs the object to move along the force.
Gravity does not move the box either. With no displacement, no force does any work.

questions.prompt: A pull does +70 J on a cart and friction does −28 J. All other forces do zero work. What is the net work?
hints: Add work contributions with their signs.

acceptedIdeas: Positive forty-two joules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is the signed sum: 70 − 28 = 42 J.

questions.onCorrect: +42 J. Net work is the signed sum of each force's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. Friction's work is negative, so it takes away from the pull's.
The pull does more work than friction takes away, so the net is positive.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Kinetic energy uses speed squared.
Use K = ½mv².
Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take half.
questions.onCorrect: 9 J. Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That squares the product of mass and speed instead of the speed alone.
That is the speed. Kinetic energy is ½mv².

questions.prompt: A cart's speed doubles while its mass stays fixed. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
hints: Mass is fixed, so only the speed term changes.
Doubling the speed doubles v before it is squared.
Square the 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies kinetic energy by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales energy with speed. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
That would be speed cubed. Energy goes as speed squared.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass doubles while its speed stays fixed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
hints: Separate the first power of mass from the square of speed.

acceptedIdeas: It doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass enters K = ½mv² as a direct multiplier, so energy doubles.

questions.onCorrect: It doubles. Mass multiplies directly in ½mv², so twice the mass is twice the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: More mass at the same speed means more energy, not less.
Squaring applies to the speed, not the mass. Doubling the mass doubles the energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on it in joules.
hints: Calculate the final and initial kinetic energies.
Net work equals their difference.
Calculate 25 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 16 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: final minus initial.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final kinetic energy alone. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object moves at speed 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Square speed before multiplying.
Use the one-half factor.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 25.
questions.onCorrect: 50 J. Square the speed, multiply by the mass, take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That uses the speed without squaring it.

questions.prompt: A cart initially has 50 J of kinetic energy and comes to rest. What net work is done on it?
hints: Use the energy change, including its sign.

acceptedIdeas: A loss of fifty joules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50 = −50 J.

questions.onCorrect: A loss of fifty joules. Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart lost energy, so the net work is negative, not a gain.
Its kinetic energy changed, so the net work is not zero. Net work equals that change.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object rises from 1 m to 5 m where g = 10 m/s². Find its gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Use the difference between final and initial height.
Multiply that difference by mg.
Calculate 3 × 10 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 120 J. The change is mass times g times the change in height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight. Multiply it by the change in height as well.
That uses the final height instead of the change in height.

questions.prompt: You shift the zero-height reference while describing the same physical rise. What happens to its gravitational potential-energy change?
hints: Only the height difference enters ΔU.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both endpoint heights shift equally, leaving both Δh and ΔU unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Both heights shift together, so the change in height does not move.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing doubles. Both end heights shift by the same amount.
The object really rises, so the change is not zero. Only the labels on the heights move.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its signed gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Final height is less than initial height.
Use final minus initial height.
Calculate 2 × 10 × (−5).
questions.onCorrect: −100 J. The object ends lower, so the change in height and the energy change are negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the object ends lower. Its potential energy falls.
That uses the starting height. Use the change in height: final minus initial.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find the work done by gravity in joules.
hints: Gravity and this displacement point the same way.
Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change.
Multiply the weight magnitude by the downward distance.
questions.onCorrect: +100 J. Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change, so a descent gives positive work.
